linkedin.body:
À l'heure où les consommateurs de produits de luxe recherchent authenticité et pérennité, la stratégie des grandes maisons s'adapte radicalement.

La transition vers ce que certains appellent le "quiet luxury" ne relève pas d'une simple esthétique passagère, mais d'une réponse économique réfléchie :
- Préservation de la valeur perçue à long terme
- Résilience face aux cycles éphémères de la fast-fashion
- Réalignement avec les valeurs d'héritage et d'artisanat d'art

Les départements presse et communication doivent désormais pivoter : valoriser la genèse des pièces, l'histoire des ateliers et la traçabilité plutôt que le simple buzz viral.

cachedArticles.title: For Clothes, Commitment Issues Are Sexy
cachedArticles.author: Highsnobiety
cachedArticles.snippet: In October 6's newsletter, in which Shopping Editor Max Migowski argues for the good in flakey fashion.
cachedArticles.content:
You're reading Shopper: Highsnobiety's bulletin on what’s taking up headspace from the marketplace. This is an edit of October 6's newsletter, in which Shopping Editor Max Migowski argues for the good in flakey fashion. Subscribe here, or head to the Shopping tab for more recs.

Fashion's Identity Crisis Isn't All Bad

Before Paris Fashion Week, a big takeaway from the Milan shows was that designers were emulating Gen Z's deliberately mismatched, thrift store-ish mode of dressing. What cynics might deem a collective identity crisis is, in actuality, an individual sartorial tapestry of interest — online and off, high-brow and low, fractured and scattered and picked at from across many tiny pockets of culture. Here, indecision and opportunism aren't a bad thing; they're creative and eclectic. Evidently, in Paris, too, the wardrobe is the only place where commitment issues are kind of sexy.

The Row, for instance, sidelined austere minimalism for something more bohemian, slightly oddball even, using rare antique laces and decorative ribbons that are hard to find and harder to replicate. By his standards, Rick Owens’ latest felt brighter and lighter than usual. Courrèges, under new leadership, felt fresh, fun, and wholly something else. Balenciaga's (rumored-to-be) last collection under Pierpaolo Piccioli was his best yet, finally exorcized of his predecessor's ghost. Tom Ford's sweater-speedo combos, half-shaven heads, and frayed pant hems with boxer shorts and ties all helped bridge the brand's vampy, sultry archetype with Haider Ackermann's more experimental vision. And Celine embodied the superlative of its Michael Rider self in convo with its Phoebe Philo past, without appearing repetitive or like some corny, cash-grabby homage.


Meanwhile, Miu Miu looks like more of the same, which certainly makes for an above-average baseline, but it no longer packs the punch it did a few seasons ago; Zara's John Galliano drop borders on costumey; Schiaparelli is stuck in a cage of its own creation; and not even a golden finale could distract from worries of what’s to happen at Saint Laurent, now that Anthony Vaccarello has (allegedly) vacated his position. These aren't negative reviews, per se, but rather an encouragement to let loose, go rogue, and try repping more than one signature theme. (Or defining one at all, as in the case of the Matières Fécales duo, whose theatrics still eclipse their product.)

It can be a good thing when customers connect a brand with a specific product or aesthetic. But it can also put that brand in a box. My favorite (and seasonally appropriate) example is Our Legacy's infamous Camion boot. It is the ultimate shoe for the plugged-in hetero fashion boy — so much so that with every new autumn and every new batch, new memes roll out as well. Still: Someone has yet to present me with a boot as perfect, as ubiquitous, and as coveted on resale sites despite everyone from Maison Margiela to COS doing their best, as you can see in our informal survey above. 


If there's a lesson to be learned, it's that getting too predictable can bite brands in the ass, but failing to convince clientele of a real POV can be just as alienating. “Be the change you wish to see,” they say, but then how about “channel the customer you wish to address,” and reflect their divided attention right back at them?

Open Tabs: Everything We've Got Our Eyes On Right Now

  • Could this leather jacket set the tone for a next Our Legacy hero product? I've certainly been seeing a lot of these torso-level pockets lately, if that's any indication…

  • I've also been seeing a lot of riffs on Red Wing Heritage's moc boots, for that matter. But why not just go with the original then? Or better yet, my favorite Norway model!

  • Since Demna is set on making kilts happen come spring, I figured Julius’ “wrapping shorts” (aka man skirt) could interest the early adopters among you.

  • For the more conservative, these black Helmut Lang wool cargos are warm, elegant, and just the right amount of edgy (and on sale!). 

  • A Kind Of Guise's double-knee, zipper-detail denim and checked down puffer pair well with one another, but are even nicer as separates to go with whatever else is in your fall/winter rotation...

  • … such as either of these Madewell pieces, perhaps? Both the fuzzy long-sleeve polo and the quarter zip sweatshirt have that weathered look I know y’all love. 

  • Anderson & Sheppard knitted the ultimate chunky cardigan. As comfortable as a blanket, as suave as a blazer. 

  • NOAH's is a lower-key, budget-friendlier version of the above: quarter of the price, not any less handsome.

  • Whalerknits x Steele is a capsule of preppy staples: two Massachusetts-based family businesses, one USA-made bundle of maritime sweaters, canvas shoppers, and homeware.

  • From the East Coast to Copenhagen via Tokyo, let's conclude with a shoutout to the Pas Normal Studios x Porter-Yoshida & Co. collaboration's standout tote. Told ya: bike fashion!

cachedArticles.title: Kim Jones's Next Move Post-Dior? $3,505 Hotel Pajamas
cachedArticles.author: Highsnobiety
cachedArticles.snippet: As other designers go fast-fashion, ex-Dior and Fendi designer Kim Jones unapologetically leans into luxury with a range of travel staples for hotel chain Aman.
cachedArticles.content:
Kim Jones knows his way around an unexpected collaboration. He was the mind behind the Louis Vuitton x Supreme run and the Dior Homme x Jordan Brand sneakers. So when Jones went free agent last year, leaving Dior after nearly a decade, it was only a matter of time until the tapped-in designer found some new way to surprise.

And surprise, he has. First came the news that he’d be creative directing a high-end sub-label of Chinese outerwear brand Bosideng. Now he’s collaborated with the ultra-luxury hotel chain Aman on a full range of ultra-luxury travel staples.

It’s a perfect pivot for someone like Jones. As designer after designer falls like a domino into positions at mass-market brands — Galliano to Zara; Marni alum Francesco Risso to GU — Jones is sticking to what he knows best: making incredibly high-end products for rich people.

Sure, the $990 black T-shirt or a pajama set totaling $3,505 may look absurd from the window-shopping masses' vantage point, but Jones has rarely left his luxury perch. And honestly? That $1,545 Aman x Kim Jones blue colorblock windbreaker is the cleanest thing he’s designed in years.

It helps that Jones also, apparently, rarely leaves the Aman ecosystem: the collection drew on his “journeys across more than 30 Aman destinations,” per the press release. Impressive, not least because a stay in an Aman hotel can run upwards of $4,000. 

This is no post-Dior “divorced dad” midlife crisis. If there’s one thing wealthy people love more than not blinking an eye at a nearly $1K T-shirt, it’s wearing said tee while staying at the hotel chain printed on its care tag, designed by someone who unapologetically leans into luxury.

Music has always played a major role in the Grand Theft Auto universe. Whether it's cruising through Los Santos with Dr. Dre and Snoop Dogg on the radio or tuning into the sounds of '80s Miami on Vice City's iconic Flash FM, Rockstar Games has made its in-game radio stations just as memorable as the worlds players explore. And for Grand Theft Auto VI, it's pulling out all the stops.

Rockstar Games has officially unveiled six of the radio stations coming to GTA VI, enlisting a stacked lineup of artists and cultural figures to serve as their hosts. Bad Bunny, Lana Del Rey, Burna Boy, Morgan Wallen, Robyn, Trick Daddy, Trina, and even Slayer's Kerry King and Tom Araya are among the names lending their voices to the game's fictional airwaves.

Each station offers its own distinct sound, reflecting the musical landscape of Leonida, the game's fictional take on Florida. Bad Bunny and RaiNao are taking over Cocoteo FM, a station dedicated to Latin music spanning bachata, merengue, dembow, and reggaeton. Meanwhile, Burna Boy and electronic producer Palms Trax will host AfroBank FM, spotlighting everything from African classics and deep cuts to contemporary amapiano and 3-step.

For Burna Boy, the opportunity marks a full-circle moment in his relationship with the franchise. Having previously appeared on GTA V's iFruit Radio with "Killin Dem" and contributed "Gettin' Money" to GTA Online's Cayo Perico update, the Nigerian superstar is now getting a station of his own.

"I've been playing GTA since way before my music ever made it into the game, so this one is personal," Burna Boy tells Hypebeast exclusively. "Then 'Killin Dem' got on iFruit Radio, we did 'Gettin' Money' for Cayo Perico, and now I have my own station in GTA VI. That whole journey is crazy to me."

"AfroBank FM is special because it gives us a space to bring our sound, our energy and our culture into a world I've been part of as a player for years," he continues. "GTA has always understood that the music is part of the world, not just something playing in the background. To now help create that world myself feels full circle."

Joining him on AfroBank FM is Palms Trax, whose selections reach beyond contemporary African hits to spotlight lesser-known records and sounds spanning generations. The station's previewed tracklist includes Asake's "Joha," Pat Thomas and Ebo Taylor's "Gye Wani," and DJ Lag and Robot Boii's "Shay'sana" featuring Kamo Mphela.

"I can't think of anything presented on this scale, musically speaking, with such a tremendous amount of perseverance and care behind it," Palms Trax tells Hypebeast. "Some of these songs have spent decades in obscurity and to see them be pride of place for one of the most anticipated audiences in the world is incredibly moving."

Like Burna Boy, Palms Trax's connection to the franchise stretches back years. "San Andreas and Vice City were some of my earliest introductions to music from outside my immediate bubble and the impact of hearing such evocative records for the first time has stayed with me ever since," he adds. "It's such a unique vehicle to capture people's imaginations and I can't wait to jump in a car and cruise around to some of the other stations."

Elsewhere across Leonida's airwaves, country music gets its own home on Back Country Radio, hosted by Morgan Wallen and Lana Del Rey, while metalheads can tune into The Chamber 106.6 with Slayer's Kerry King and Tom Araya. Robyn and model Alex Consani are bringing pop hits from the likes of Charli xcx, MGMT, and Zara Larsson to the returning Flash FM, while Miami rap legends Trick Daddy and Trina will hold down Dirty South Classics, spinning Southern hip-hop staples from David Banner, JT Money, and more.

But the radio stations aren't the only new addition to GTA VI's musical universe. For the first time in the franchise's history, Rockstar is introducing on-demand podcasts, alongside the ability for protagonists Jason and Lucia to listen to music and podcasts outside of vehicles through headphones and earbuds connected to their in-game smartphones.

Rockstar is promising its biggest and most diverse radio lineup to date, with additional stations spanning classic rock, blues, electronic, talk radio, and more still to be revealed. Details surrounding the game's dynamic score and additional singles from 'Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album' are also on the way.

Listen to Hypebeast's exclusive stream of AfroBank FM above, and head over to the official Grand Theft Auto VI website to preview the remaining stations ahead of the game's November 19 release on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S.

cachedArticles.title: What Makes Langston Uibel’s Sole Bounce?
cachedArticles.author: Highsnobiety
cachedArticles.snippet: With Bouncing Soles is now the brand’s new global platform, asking Chloë Sevigny, Jordan Stephens, Naomi Watanabe and Germany’s Langston Uibel what keeps them moving.⁠ For Uibel, it’s theatre, film and finding his place as an artist. Learn more about the actor, here.
cachedArticles.content:
If you have ever owned a pair of Doc’s, you already know the words: “With Bouncing Soles.”

They have appeared on Dr. Martens’ heel loops since the first 1460 boot rolled off the production line in 1960. Originally a reference to the brand’s air-cushioned sole, those three words are now the foundation of its new global platform, connecting product, craft and culture through one question: What makes your sole bounce?

For AW26, Dr. Martens is putting that question to creative figures around the world. Chloë Sevigny finds her bounce in curiosity, Jordan Stephens in words, and Naomi Watanabe in joy and comedy. In Germany, actor Langston Uibel brings his own answer to the mix.

Right now, what gets Uibel up and moving is a packed run of theatre and film. He is rehearsing Chekhov’s The Seagull at Schauspielhaus Düsseldorf, premiering on October 16, while working across several film projects, including Hijack, Sentimental Fail Club or Hyper Baby.

“I really feel like I’m at a point where I’ve found my voice and found my place as an artist,” he says. “I just want to prove to everybody that I can do it.”

That sense of self runs through everything Uibel does. He pushes back against the pressure to perform one fixed version of authenticity, describing himself instead as “a smaller or a larger version of me, depending on the situation.” Acting, clothing and daily life are not separate categories. Every choice is part of the same picture.

“Nothing is ever a coincidence,” he explains. “That choice could be a line in a script, a choice I make in acting, or the trainers I put on in the morning.”

It is fitting, then, that Uibel did more than appear in Dr. Martens’ German campaign. He also executive produced it, developing the idea while walking through Berlin and London in his Crazy Horse leather Doc’s.

The leather sits at the center of the AW26 collection, covering five Dr. Martens signatures: the 1460 boot, 1461 shoe, Adrian loafer, 2976 Chelsea boot and 8065 Mary Jane. A new Cherry Red finish joins the line-up, while the 1460, 1461 and 8065 also arrive in DM’s Green.

Designed to pick up creases, scuffs and patina over time, Crazy Horse becomes more individual with every wear. For Uibel, that personalization is the point. He sees Doc’s across every part of society, worn by people who otherwise have little in common. Few shoes can move between scenes without being claimed by only one.

So, what really makes his sole bounce? The answer changes. It might be performing to a thousand people at Vienna’s Burgtheater, meeting an artist who sees his full potential or simply watching Hertha BSC fight its way back into the first league.

“At the end of the day,” he says, “it’s West Berlin for life.”

In the quiet stillness of a New York morning, Justin Boone fastens a silver chain before reaching into his wardrobe. For the creative director, stylist, and vintage brand founder, getting dressed is a ritual rooted in personal identity. “When I’m getting dressed in the morning, fit, fabric, and function—like those are my three pillars,” Justin reflects, adjusting his beanie before stepping into a light-filled living room where his young daughter and son play across the carpet. His personal style is refined yet deeply grounded in the lived-in reality of fatherhood.



Becoming a parent didn't narrow his sartorial eye; it expanded his appreciation for pieces that carry real utility and character. "Fatherhood changed my style," Justin says, crouching down on the rug to hand a toy to his daughter. "I feel like the things that I wear now, I’m not afraid of getting dirty. They’re utilitarian, so I can do almost anything. Vintage pieces to me feel special when you can see somewhat of a life that was lived through them, and that’s what I try to emulate in my own clothing as well—designing pieces that make people want to live in their clothes."



Between managing design deadlines and family moments, the red Target bag becomes the quiet anchor of his daily movement. It is an extension of his utilitarian ethos, sitting comfortably in the trunk of his vintage BMW, hanging off an exterior balcony chair, or resting beside his laptop on a workstation. The bag doesn't act as a forced fashion statement; instead, its bold bullseye pattern complements his double-denim aesthetic while serving as an indispensable tool for his multi-faceted day.



“Navigating through life as a dad, as a father, as a creative director, my biggest essential is a tote bag,” Justin explains as he walks down a city street, tote in hand. “I know that when I have my bag with me, dump anything that I need in it—some diapers, wipes, a juice box, my notebook, a really good set of pens that I got from Target actually, and I always like to have a camera on me. If anybody needs anything, I have it.”

Whether blowing bubbles on the living room floor with his daughter or stepping out to head into a busy afternoon of creative direction, the tote bridges the gap between home and work. It carries the tools of his trade right alongside the everyday essentials of fatherhood. As Justin loads his vintage car and heads out into the city, the tote proves that style is about carrying every part of your life along with you.

cachedArticles.content:
Summary

'State of Art' is a new HypeArt series inviting artists, curators, collectors and other leading voices to weigh in on the ideas, debates and cultural shifts shaping contemporary art. Through intimate questions and personal recommendations, the series offers a closer look at what is exciting the art world, what needs to change and where things may be heading next.

For artists today, visibility no longer depends on being discovered by a gallery. Social media has collapsed many of the barriers that once separated artists from collectors, curators and audiences, while direct sales and self-organized exhibitions have made it increasingly possible to build a career outside the traditional gallery system.

For Destinee Ross-Sutton, that does not mean galleries have become obsolete. It means they have to prove their value. “I don’t think every artist needs a gallery,” the Harlem-born curator and founder of Ross-Sutton Gallery tells Hypeart. “But I do know the right gallery can be an essential partner.”

In the latest edition of 'State of Art,' Ross-Sutton considers what representation actually means in 2026, from the shifting power dynamic between artists and dealers to the increasingly contested 50-percent gallery commission.

Social media, she argues, has fundamentally changed the entire landscape. Artists can now introduce their work to thousands of people without waiting for a dealer, critic or curator to grant them access. They can watch their own markets develop in real time, identify collectors and, at a rapid fire pace, sell work directly.

"Galleries are no longer really the gatekeepers" – Destinee Ross-Sutton

But visibility, she stresses, should not be confused with longevity. A serious career requires an infrastructure that extends far beyond finding a buyer. At its best, a gallery provides strategy, trusted relationships, institutional access and an understanding of how decisions made today might affect an artist five or ten years down their career.

“A good gallery is thinking several years ahead,” she explains. “It isn’t simply about where the next work is going to sell. It’s about the best place for the art, which collections it enters, which exhibitions and institutions make sense, how the market develops responsibly and how the artist’s practice is protected as their presence grows.”

That distinction is particularly important as artists reconsider why they should continue surrendering as much as half of a sale to a gallery when they may already have direct access to interested collectors. For Ross-Sutton, the percentage only makes sense when the gallery is doing significantly more than facilitating a transaction. Exhibitions, production, shipping, fairs, press, collector development and museum relationships are all part of the gallery package. The real measure, she says, is not the immediate sale but what that sale helps build around the artist.

Independent careers are increasingly viable as well. But Ross-Sutton points out that many artists operating successfully without conventional representation have effectively constructed galleries of their own, surrounding themselves with studio managers and teams responsible for administration, exhibitions, collectors and institutions.

“Independence doesn’t mean doing everything alone"

The more pressing concern, then, may be what happens when representation becomes transactional rather than developmental. Ross-Sutton distinguishes between galleries that stay committed to an artist through the inevitable fluctuations of a career and those that arrive when demand peaks, capitalize on sales and disappear when momentum slows. For her, representation carries an obligation to understand not only the work, but the person and cultural context behind it.

She recalls a South African artist with an international career spanning nearly three decades who told Ross-Sutton that hers was the first gallery to actually travel to South Africa to meet her and better understand her practice.

"How can you properly advocate for an artist if you haven’t made the effort to understand where the work comes from?"

That philosophy also extends beyond a gallery’s own program. In 2020, Ross-Sutton curated ‘BLACK VOICES/BLACK MICROCOSM’ in Stockholm, bringing together 31 artists from across the Black diaspora and intentionally dissolving distinctions between emerging and established artists, formal and self-taught practices and differing levels of market recognition.

She encountered a recurring problem there, and later while curating ‘Unapologetic WomXn: The Dream Is the Truth’ in Venice: artists who wanted to participate but whose galleries resisted allowing them to do so. The latter exhibition ultimately brought together more than 30 women artists during the 60th Venice Biennale.

For Ross-Sutton, protecting an artist’s career should never become synonymous with controlling it. “There is a difference between representing an artist and possessing an artist,” she says. “Sometimes an opportunity outside your own walls may be exactly what is right for that artist’s career.”

It leads to the question at the center of her argument: “Is the relationship there to serve the artist’s career, or is the artist there to serve the gallery?” If Ross-Sutton were an emerging artist now, representation would still be a goal, but only under the right circumstances. She would want to know whether a gallery understood the work, who its collectors were, what institutional relationships it could offer, whether it welcomed outside opportunities and, crucially, whether it would remain invested when sales were not immediate.

“I would rather have no gallery than the wrong gallery,” she says. “But the right relationship can still be transformative.”

Summary

Wren introduced the Vessel, a futuristic integrated-bracelet 904L steel watch.It features a world-first sapphire crystal with mirrored top-and-bottom curved facets.Limited to 300 pieces total, prices start at $2,900 USD.

Wren is moving beyond the dive-watch category with The Vessel, a new integrated-bracelet sports watch that marks a significant expansion of the young New York independent’s design language.

Founded in 2024 and previously known for limited-run divers such as the Diver 38 Mad and Diver One Abyss, Wren approached the Vessel with a deliberately forward-looking brief: create a sports watch that feels inspired by 2075 rather than 1975. Founder Craig Karger brought in British watch designer Max Resnick - whose recent work includes Anoma and VPC - to develop the project, marking the first time Wren has collaborated with an outside designer. After roughly two years of development, the resulting 39mm cushion-shaped, stainless-steel case moves away from familiar integrated-bracelet templates while building the entire architecture around one defining component: its unusually complex sapphire crystal.

Rather than treating faceted sapphire as a decorative finishing touch, the Vessel uses a crystal with matching curved facets cut into both its exterior and underside, with the internal surface acting as a precise negative of the geometry above. According to Wren, this mirrored construction is intended to prevent the dial distortion that can occur when a faceted outer crystal is paired with a flat or conventionally domed underside.

Developing it proved particularly challenging: an early prototype batch yielded only five usable crystals out of 100 before Wren eventually partnered with a specialist sapphire-case manufacturer capable of producing the required form. The same bespoke approach extends to the bracelet, which features Wren’s own quick-release mechanism and a micro-adjustment system integrated directly into the links rather than the clasp. Two dial options will be offered - a steel sunray version and a meteorite edition - both accented by an aqua seconds hand and matching aqua movement rotor, a visual callback to Wren’s inaugural Diver One Aqua.

Behind the open caseback sits a Sellita SW300-1 automatic movement, running at 28,800 vph with a 56-hour power reserve, while the watch offers 70 meters of water resistance and measures 10.6mm thick. The Vessel launches in two strictly limited references of 150 pieces each, with neither configuration planned for reproduction after the initial run. The steel sunray dial version is priced at $2,900 USD, while the meteorite model is $3,400 USD. Pre-orders are now open through Wren’s website, with deliveries scheduled for Q1 2027.

The Samba has had plenty of lives over the years, but this might be one of its more handsome ones. adidas has given the familiar low-top a decidedly fall-ready treatment, swapping out the usual smooth upper for something a little more textured.

The adidas Samba OG gets dressed up in herringbone tweed, and honestly, it suits the old favorite rather well.

The Samba has done the minimalist thing. It’s had its fashion moment. Now it’s getting a little more textured and considerably more interesting.

NOMOS is cooling down its Metro collection with two new “Ice Blue” references, translating the line’s urban design language into a pale metallic finish inspired by contemporary glass-and-steel architecture.

Designed by Berlin-based product designer Mark Braun, Metro has balanced precision, negative space and playful color since its introduction in 2014, when the original Metro Date Power Reserve became the first NOMOS watch equipped with the manufacture’s proprietary swing system escapement. The new Metro Date Power Reserve Ice Blue and Metro neomatik 41 Update Ice Blue retain those familiar codes while shifting the palette toward light blue, teal and muted grey, with galvanized dials that move from cool blue to nearly white depending on the surrounding light.

The Metro Date Power Reserve Ice Blue, reference 1121, comes in a compact 37mm stainless-steel case measuring just 8mm thick, pairing its metallic dial with blue and white dot indexes, grey minute numerals and a tri-color power reserve indicator rendered in white, light blue and teal. More significantly, it debuts the new hand-wound DUW 4701, replacing the DUW 4401 used by the original 2014 model. The 2.8mm-thick in-house movement delivers a 52-hour power reserve and patented quick-set date, while its sapphire caseback reveals a skeletonized balance cock, NOMOS perlage, gold engravings and sunburst decoration surrounding the swing system.

The larger Metro neomatik 41 Update Ice Blue, reference 1166, measures 40.5mm across and 9.1mm thick, using the automatic DUW 6101 with a 48-hour reserve. Its signature ring-date display places the entire month around the dial perimeter, with two teal markers framing the current date, while a woven waterproof grey textile strap reinforces the cooler, more technical aesthetic.

The two Ice Blue models broaden the Metro family without departing from its minimalist character: the 37mm version emphasizes traditional hand-wound mechanics and the collection’s asymmetric power-reserve display, while the 40.5mm neomatik offers automatic winding and a more graphic approach to the date. cachedArticles.content:
The Samba Jane has already put a different spin on the classic Samba, but this version takes things somewhere a little more wild. Specifically, the countryside.

The adidas Samba Jane comes covered in a textured cow print, turning an otherwise familiar silhouette into something with a lot more to moo about.

The black and white pattern is mottled and fuzzy, giving the upper a tactile feel that you don’t usually associate with the classic terrace. It’s a pretty funny way to dress up such a recognizable sneaker, but hey, it’s working.

Then there’s the Jane part. A strap across the foot replaces the usual laces, giving the low-slung silhouette its Mary Jane treatment. It makes the Samba feel a little sweeter, while the cow print pulls it in the opposite direction.

And that contrast is what makes this version work. You’ve still got the Three Stripes and the usual shape, but the textured upper completely changes the moo(d). It takes something you’ve seen countless times and makes it feel a little less obvious. The cow print is obviously doing most of the talking, but the Mary Jane strap keeps it from becoming too novelty-driven.

It’s also the kind of sneaker that doesn’t need much else going on. The black and white upper is easy enough to wear, while the texture gives it enough personality to carry an outfit on its own. You could keep everything else pretty simple and let the sneakers do what they clearly came here to do.

So, no, a cow-print Samba Jane probably wasn’t on your radar. But it should be. There’s something about taking one of the most recognizable sneakers around and giving it a slightly unhinged countryside makeover that makes the whole thing feel surprisingly fresh. Consider this your sign to let a little farmyard energy into the rotation.

Plaster has joined forces with London-based artist Soldier, real name Leonard Iheagwam, to bring his latest set of artwork to life at their collaborative exhibition titled "Military Abstractions”.

Launching ahead of Frieze London, Soldier’s exhibition will span across the first two floors of Plaster’s HQ in Soho. The exhibit acts as an extension of Plaster's ongoing mission of platforming young artists and bridging the gap between the art community through in-person events. Born in Lagos, Nigeria, Soldier has been building himself as one of the most exciting voices growing within the London art scene.

Frequently reflecting on his personal experience, Soldier pulls inspiration from Lagos' skateboarding scene, church and Military surplus, which materialize through various visual signatures. “Military Abstractions” explores Soldier’s staple motifs, including camouflage and toy soldiers, which act as a visual portrayal of geopolitical and military power, researching deeper into the consequences of war and foreign influence on countries that have experienced colonization. Camouflage is reclaimed from its original connotations and transformed through collages central to Soldier’s personal perspective and artistic practice.

Four out of the six new large-scale artworks set to be on display will be available for sale alongside signed posters and limited-edition T-shirts. An exclusive release of 50 original editions are also scheduled for online purchase via a registration-only drop, set to launch simultaneously with the private viewing.

It's an exciting collaboration between Plaster and Soldier that will bring together the art world, celebrating young artists expanding out of London.

cachedArticles.title: State of the Art: Jonathan Anderson's Next Power Move Has Nothing to Do With Dior
cachedArticles.author: Highsnobiety
cachedArticles.snippet: Jonathan Anderson's art show at his JWA Pimlico flagship store for Frieze establishes the designer as a cultural force unconstrained by any one fashion house.
cachedArticles.content:
In State of the Art, a column for Highsnobiety, Chris Erik Thomas untangles the crossover between fashion and art.

Jonathan Anderson has never felt like a traditional fashion designer. His brain is simply too big; his curiosity is too strong to stay constrained to one medium. So it wasn’t surprising to hear that just days after showing the Dior Spring/Summer 2027 runway collection at Paris Fashion Week, he’s already sorted his follow-up show — and it has nothing to do with fashion. 

"'A Composition,' a new group art exhibition in partnership with Platinum Card by American Express," sees the designer curate works by four artists at his JW Anderson flagship store. Timed to Frieze London and opening to the public on October 15, the stretchily titled, corporate-backed show confirms Anderson’s status as a cultural force on par with the likes of Miuccia Prada. (She also works between two fashion brands and has deep art-world ties.)

The show will feature a new series of 30 wind chimes by Cerith Wyn Evans made specifically for the brand, plus ceramics by Akiko Hirai, paintings by Mary Stephenson, and sculptures by Shawanda Corbett. It’s an interesting mix, but focusing on how their respective mediums meld would miss the point, which is that this isn’t just Anderson curating another exhibition (he’s done a handful) or even the first show at the JWA Pimlico space — it’s a power move.

Anderson helped launch the Loewe Craft Prize and holds the keys to one of fashion’s biggest luxury houses at Dior (and has done countless artist collabs between both brands). Yet the cultural capital of his name has developed a strength all its own, built on relationships that aren’t siloed to any one label. 

Crucially, each of these artists has already staked out a spot in Anderson’s orbit: Stephenson modeled for the JW Anderson Resort Spring 2026 collection, and her paintings were hung in the Pimlico space for its 2025 opening; Wyn Evans did a series of lights for Loewe Lamps at Milan Design Week in 2024; Corbett did a series of limited edition JWA blankets in 2021; and Hirai’s pottery has been regularly displayed in JWA stores since 2020. The common thread isn’t a brand; it’s Jonathan Anderson. 

The dividing line between creative fields like fashion and art has always been flimsy, but few modern figures have worked as hard to dismantle those boundaries as he has. A group show that feels more like a meetup of a few of his favorite artists — held in a shop that sells artisanal Welsh blankets and 19th-century French watering cans alongside twisted denim pants and poplin shirts — affirms it.

The Samba didn’t need another colorway, but this one makes a pretty strong case for existing anyway. The combination of deep brown and coffee-colored details look almost suspiciously good on the familiar silhouette.

The adidas Samba OG comes in Dusky Bronze, Aurora Coffee, and Gum, giving the terrace classic a much richer personality than its usual black-and-white uniform.

The Samba is hardly a rogue sneaker at this point. That makes a genuinely good colorway all the more important.

This one has the colors, the gum sole and just enough obscurity to make an old favorite feel worth looking at again.

cachedArticles.title: These Champion Sweats Took a Mud Bath in Japan
cachedArticles.author: Highsnobiety
cachedArticles.snippet: What could be better than mud-dyed Champion shirts? How about vintage-inspired sweats with vintage-looking dyes to match?
cachedArticles.content:
The beauty of a mud-dyed Champion sweater is that it's simply wrong. The perfect retro sportswear pullover is soft and nice, something you could actually imagine being worn for workouts a half-century ago. Dipping it in mud until its surface resembles something like, well, mud would seem to defeat the purpose.

And that's exactly the appeal.

I am inextricably drawn towards anything that elevates the ordinary into something special. This is the entire framework behind our mantra of "good clothes" you know: transforming the normal into the beautiful. There's also a dab of Duchamp at play, especially when someone like Sashiko Gals is out here treating mass-produced sneakers like art.

Dipping a Champion sweater in mud is the exact kind of contradiction I love.

And this ain't your average mud. This is the historic dorozome mud-dye of Japan's Amami Oshima island, an ancient technique that makes quite literally everything look cool.

And I especially appreciate that the two styles of Champion shirt that received the treatment were also part of Champion Japan's Made in America program, so you have a real East-meets-West moment, if you'll excuse the cliche. (although Champion Japan is domestically operated by apparel giant Itochu.)

Around the same time as these tasty T-shirt contradictions, the Hiroshi Fujiwara co-helmed project Various Artists delivered a quartet of specially treated Champion sweats sewn to the specifications of vintage models and specially dyed to look the part. Again, artisanal approach meets ordinary object. I love it.

I don't even love those old-school Champion sweats — too narrow for my tastes — but I do appreciate the fastidiousness in taking a plain object to the next level.

It's a matter of taste, of identifying something good and going the extra mile to make it that much better. No complications, just good clothes.

Summary

Prada expands its circular fashion initiatives with Re-Cashmere and Re-Wool.Recycled fibers become refined knitwear, tailored separates and everyday wardrobe staples.Made in Italy, the collections feature limited production quantities and NFC-enabled traceability.

Prada has expanded its ongoing commitment to sustainable circularity with the debut of its Re-Cashmere and Re-Wool initiatives, translating the eco-minded ethos behind Re-Nylon into natural animal fibers. These projects focus upstream by gathering pre-consumer offcuts, spinning residues, and factory surplus directly from Prada Group facilities, such as its knitwear site in Torgiano, Italy.

The collected fibers are sorted by color to bypass additional chemical dyeing processes before being carded and spun into new yarns. To ensure complete transparency, every garment is embedded with an NFC tag linked to the Aura Blockchain Consortium platform, granting customers digital certificates of authenticity and end-to-end traceability detailing supply chain processing stages and fiber origin.

Crafted entirely in Italy across specialized workshops in Tuscany and Umbria, the collection centers on timeless, layerable ready-to-wear built for everyday wearability. Re-Cashmere - constructed from 100% GRS-certified recycled cashmere and SFA-certified sustainable raw inputs - takes shape as refined men's and women's sweaters. Meanwhile, Re-Wool blends RWS-certified virgin wool with recycled wool and cashmere through a specialized wet shredding technique, yielding structured trousers, blouson jackets, skirts, and dresses. Because production relies strictly on available factory remnants, every piece is inherently limited in quantity.

The Prada Re-Cashmere & Re-Wool collection officially debuted this part as part of the FW26 range and is available now globally via Prada.com and select Prada boutiques

Sony Pictures Entertainment has launched Crunchyroll Storyworks, a new division designed to develop anime and live-action adaptations in closer collaboration with Japan’s creative industry. Announced by Sony Pictures Entertainment Chairman and CEO Ravi Ahuja during the inaugural Crunchyroll Anime Future Forum in New York, the unit will operate within Crunchyroll’s content group and work in both directions: adapting stories from around the world into anime while developing Japanese anime properties for live-action film and television.

The groundwork for this creative expansion was laid in March 2025 with the formation of HAYATE, a Tokyo-based production joint venture co-founded by Aniplex and Crunchyroll.

Originally established to fuse Aniplex’s industry-leading production expertise with Crunchyroll’s massive global distribution network, HAYATE will now work in tandem with the newly minted Storyworks division. Crunchyroll Storyworks will serve as the developmental engine, identifying, planning, and accelerating projects before passing them over to HAYATE and its partner Japanese studios for physical production. Summary

6:AM launches "Batch," a modular glass collection originally debuted with Bottega Veneta.The 43cm cubes feature undulating textures created via CNC-engraved cast-iron molds.Available in ten colors, the pieces build luminous architectural surfaces.

6:AM continues its exploration of glass as an architectural material with “Batch,” a modular collection that pushes Murano craftsmanship beyond the scale of the standalone object. First publicly presented during Milan Design Week 2026 and originally developed in collaboration with Bottega Veneta for its Summer 2026 show, the project revolves around a single 43cm x 43cm x 43 cm blown-glass cube. Produced using a cast-iron mold engraved through CNC technology, each module is shaped through a subtractive process that 6:AM likens to the rough-hewing of marble, gradually revealing the form rather than building it up. Even its name draws directly from glassmaking: “batch” refers to the mixture of raw ingredients loaded into a furnace before melting, turning the collection’s production method into both its technical foundation and conceptual starting point.

Where earlier presentations introduced the cube as the project’s fundamental building block, “Batch” expands that language through repetition, allowing a single glass object to become an architectural surface. For its latest presentation, 126 modules are assembled on a pared-back steel framework to create a tall, translucent plane. The softly rippled surfaces retain traces of the blowing process, bending and scattering light into shifting reflections and distortions as viewers move around the installation. Colored cubes interrupt the otherwise transparent grid, introducing moments of saturation that ripple visually across the structure. The result sits somewhere between sculpture, partition and architectural intervention: an orderly modular system whose handmade irregularities prevent it from ever feeling entirely uniform.

The collection also develops the modular idea through an expanded palette of 10 color variations: Cristallo, Terra, Rubino, Bianco, Verde Chiaro, Verde Antico, Ambra Scuro, Nero, Acciaio and Rosso. Together, the finishes underline 6:AM’s ongoing approach of pairing traditional Murano glassmaking with contemporary industrial processes, while giving the cube enough flexibility to operate as an individual object or as part of a larger spatial composition. In that sense, “Batch” extends the thinking established through its earlier Bottega Veneta iteration, shifting attention from a singular sculptural gesture toward a repeatable system capable of interacting with architecture, light and space. The 6:AM “Batch” collection is available now through the brand’s website.

Skydance Corporation shares fell 8% to $8.79 USD on Wednesday, following the formal closure of the historic merger combining Paramount and Warner Bros. The stock drop occurred on the newly formed media conglomerate's second day of trading on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker SKYD.

cachedArticles.content:
You just know an unaccessorized bike just hates to see PORTER comin’. The Japanese heritage brand is no stranger to cycling gear, thanks to its seven-year-strong collaboration with Copenhagen’s most fashionable biker brand, Pas Normal Studios. But the duo’s latest release feels like a step up from the normal (albeit incredibly well-crafted) backpacks and messenger bags that we’re used to seeing. 

The sixth Pas x PORTER collection still has bags for real human bodies, to be clear, but this iteration also extends the on-bike offerings beyond the strappy saddle bag.

There are now also bags for the frame and the handlebars — effectively turning any ole two-wheeler into a steezy, Japanese-inflected whip. After five solid collabs, this feels like the next logical step toward turning the actual cycle into the next best way to signal you know your shit. (Or, at the very least, know that PORTER is a military-grade bag GOAT.)

The release is a fitting cap on a particularly cycle-centric summer at PORTER. It released a four-piece collection with Canadian menswear label JJJJound in July, a first-ever linkup that included a great ripstop nylon city bag. And if that connection feels familiar, it should. JJJJound’s first real dip into cycling gear arrived last year with none other than Pas Normal Studios.

Call it the byproduct of very productive business card swapping, if you will, but these brands all get that bike apparel isn’t just for gearheads anymore. Pas staked a foothold in the market by turning cycling into something fashionable, while JJJJound is just fashionable full-stop. With PORTER now doing collabs with both brands, it's clear the old, storied Japanese bagmaker is plenty comfortable in the bike lane.

cachedArticles.title: Did Issey Miyake Design These Brooklyn Teachers’ Uniforms?
cachedArticles.author: Highsnobiety
cachedArticles.snippet: A Brooklyn Montessori school seems to outfit its staff in Pleats Please.
cachedArticles.content:
A school whose teachers’ uniforms are…Issey Miyake? Sounds too good to be true — because it kinda is. A post on r/Williamsburg titled ‘Issey Miyake Kindergarten?’ went viral last night over whispers that a local Montessori school supplied its employees with full Pleats Please looks. News of the Issey-dripped teachers quickly spread to Twitter, where the official staff photo in question dropped and, hey, it really does look like they’re wearing Issey. At least at first glance. While some users speculated on whether or not the image is AI-generated, most agreed the staff just have that shit on. 

This morning, Ms. Lam Montessori — a Mandarin-immersion Montessori school with three locations across Brooklyn — took to Instagram to both respond to the love and dispel the myth: the teachers are real people, and the uniforms are not Issey Miyake, but come from a “different Japanese brand with a similar look at a more affordable price,” to quote their story post.

The brand in question is Takashi Yamasaki, a Taiwanese label whose pleated garments do sort of resemble the late Miyake’s most famous imprint. Its website shows a lot of pieces that resemble Pleats Please essentials, like a long tank dress, elastic-waist slim leg pants, and round-sleeve t-shirt silhouettes all in pre-pleated colorful forms. But there are also a lot of departures that show Yamasaki’s own pleated styling, like this wrinkled-on-purpose vest (as in, British-English for “tank top”) with a smocked collar and waist hem. 

Pleats Please pieces from Issey Miyake usually hover around $400, with some rare or museum-grade items priced as high as $2.5k (This AW96 Yasumasa Morimura collab top is currently top of my Grailed watchlist). Yamasaki pieces, however, stay in the $1,273–$4,777 TWD range ($40–$150 USD), like. his dolman sleeve blouse priced at $1,528 TWD ($48 USD). For perspective, that’s about 14.29 percent of the cost of an actual Pleats Please top. 

Ms. Lam Montessori’s Instagram story also mentioned that its staff wear these pleated garments for similar reasoning behind Issey Miyake’s original Pleats Please concept: flexibility, both in concept and practice. The fabric is machine-washable, doesn’t wrinkle, and is adaptable to multiple climates hot or cold with proper layering.

Most importantly for a teacher, especially a Montessori teacher whose day is to facilitate tactile learning, pleats are durable. It really only makes sense that Montessori teachers, especially ones in Brooklyn, would adopt the pleats manifesto into their education. Flexible clothing for building flexible minds, Issey would be proud.

cachedArticles.title: For JBadvss, Fashion is a Feeling
cachedArticles.author: Highsnobiety
cachedArticles.snippet: Taking cues from a heritage brand like UGG, Jay Perez leans on instinct rather than expectation when getting dressed.
cachedArticles.content:
In New York City, street style is an ever-present — almost unavoidable — part of its culture, deeply influencing someone like Jay Perez, who grew up navigating its countless blocks and avenues. Known these days mostly by his online moniker, JBadvss, Perez recalls his neighborhood corner being the epicenter for his early interactions with fashion. 

Raised in Dyckman, the famed Upper Manhattan neighborhood, the new-age style purveyor leaned on figures like his older brothers and community OGs to shape his early understanding of what “getting fly” really meant — and what it looked like in practice. 

“I’m the youngest of my brothers, so I was looking up at them and the dudes they were hanging out with when I was a kid,” Perez says. “They always looked super neat and clean. It was an energy more than anything.” 

While Perez resonated with the spirit of how they put their looks together, his personal aesthetic drastically differed from that of his stylistic role models. For him, fashion is about taking risks, pushing boundaries, and making people reconsider previously held notions — all while still feeling like the “freshest out.” 

Through the years, Perez and his friends pioneered a lane of their own. Drawing inspiration from the maximal West Coast flavors of the early 2010s — known in certain internet circles as the “Swag Era” — the collective began experimenting with shape and proportion, even going so far as to challenge conventional ideas about gendered clothing. 

“I love pretty boy stuff,” he shares candidly. “I like kilts, skirts, painting my nails. If I could have worn a wig like Prince, I would. I just love a little extra-ness. When I get dressed, I want to try something different. I don't care if people don't put on some shit in a certain way, as long as I think it's cool, I’m going to rock it.”

This unabashed trailblazing ethos guided Perez toward looks and brands that matched his vision of what fashion can be, with UGG as a mainstay throughout that evolution. Built on the idea that comfort can unlock confidence, UGG is one of contemporary fashion’s most pervasive disruptors, using its classic silhouettes to help redefine the landscape. But for someone like Perez, it’s just another part of getting dressed. 

“People didn’t understand that everything is unisex,” he argues. “That’s why UGG has always gone hand in hand with my style. It’s just about showing people that anybody can wear anything, and freak it in their own way.” 

Never letting stray comments or opinions shake his personal agency, Perez has since established himself as a daring force willing to shake things up while putting looks together in ways most might not have considered. With a substantial online following for his avant-garde, expressive tastes, Perez carries the mantle of forebears like UGG, subverting expectations in his own way. 

Laced in the brand’s Birch Boot II, Perez offers a tangible look at how his approach overlaps with the UGG brand’s heritage, embracing instinct over safety and conformity. Dressed in a look that feels bold yet collected and comfortable, Perez shows a clear understanding of how to bend style to his will — subtly abstracting familiar visual motifs through his own stylistic lens. This playful framework disregards outside constraints and offers Perez the liberty to do as he pleases while assembling an outfit. 

“I’m a little delusional with everything,” he shares with a smile. “I know I can pull anything off, and I’m always visualizing what my outfits will look like. Sometimes I see myself as a video game character in my own head.” 

Taking things to the next level, Perez and UGG continue to serve as distinct examples of what happens when you hang up convention and let your imagination take the lead, proving that personal style is at its best when there is room to explore, evolve, and simply lean into what feels right — even if it looks wrong to some, for now.

cachedArticles.title: Teenage Engineering Is Going to Stop Making Synths
cachedArticles.author: Highsnobiety
cachedArticles.snippet: Founder Jesper Kouthoofd says the pivot is part of the enigmatic Swedish company’s plan to stay fresh.
cachedArticles.content:
“What you do when you’re 10 is what you should be doing when you’re grown up,” Jesper Kouthoofd says a few minutes into our conversation. He makes it sound self-evident, but it says a lot about teenage engineering, the Stockholm-based electronics and design company he founded in 2005. 

Over two decades, teenage engineering has built a worldwide following among musicians and producers, from aspiring hobbyists to A-listers such as Travis Scott, Sabrina Carpenter, and Kevin Parker. Its almost magical appeal lies less in products, marketing, or strategy than in Kouthoofd’s attempt to scale the fascinations of his childhood self into a sizable business. 

As romantic as that may sound, it has very real consequences, including decisions few CEOs would seriously consider. Just how far Kouthoofd is willing to take his philosophy becomes clear when Kouthoofd tells me that, as part of a reorganization last fall, he announced to his team he is planning to stop making synthesizers altogether. The OP-1 is no exception. Launched in 2011, it put teenage engineering on the map and has been central to its success ever since. 

“Everyone was like, ‘What are you talking about?’ But I’ve come to the conclusion that, for us, the products aren’t the business,” Kouthoofd says. “We can be so much more than that.”  

It’s this kind of thinking that has made teenage engineering the enigmatic company it is. “We have a lot of haters because we tend to disturb people’s minds,” Kouthoofd says with a laugh. Anyone who’s spent time in the teenage engineering corner of the internet is familiar with the fascination — and the buzz — it generates. YouTube is full of reviews, technical breakdowns, and longform explainers on the company. On Reddit, threads with titles such as “Can someone please explain teenage engineering to me?” run to hundreds of replies. Some users offer cultural shorthand: “They’re the Apple of the music world.” Others are more acerbic: “They’re just a bunch of rich guys in a room thinking: throw it at a wall, if it sticks, charge $1500 for it.” 

The products that teenage engineering puts out combine minimalist industrial design with a quirky, almost childlike sense of humor. There’s everything from audio equipment to a portable vinyl record cutter, a tape dispenser, and a $2,000 choir of eight wooden dolls singing choral classics. The OP-1 is known for its cartoonish user interface. It features a cow whose four stomachs visualize different delay effects; launching the sequencer shows the phrase “Marx was right.” One groovebox, the EP-1320, uses Old English fonts and Latin labels and comes preloaded with hundreds of medieval samples, including lutes and Gregorian chants. 

“Often,” Kouthoofd says, “when a product may not be reasonable or probably won’t be profitable, it’s good to just put it out there, see what happens.” That same mentality lets teenage engineering move easily from a sampler with Supreme and a DJ deck designed for the late Virgil Abloh to products that end up on bedroom desks and in home studios. As one Reddit user puts it: “Maybe teenage engineering is a collective of ingenious yet devious trolls who exist solely to make the online community seethe.”  

When I read that comment to Kouthoofd, he laughs. The mischievous look in his eyes reminds me of my high school chemistry teacher who loved proving that people only call something a miracle when they don’t understand how it works. Kouthoofd and I have just sat down on two big black floor chairs at teenage engineering’s headquarters in Hammarby Sjöstad, a former industrial waterfront transformed into a showcase of Scandinavian urban planning. “There’s no hidden secret to what all this is,” he says, pointing to a table covered in teenage engineering products, some yet released. “In fact, it’s almost too obvious. I’m the son of a Dutch architect father and a Swedish banking mother. I grew up watching him draw and her doing big business. Honestly, I see myself as the perfect 50/50 combination of my parents.” 

These days, at 56, Kouthoofd is the CEO of a company with roughly 100 employees and annual revenues of around $46 million. He has enough resources and experience to run it exactly the way he wants — as an extension of childhood Saturdays spent building electric kits from the local store in a village on Sweden’s west coast. 

Kouthoofd is an unconventional leader. He doesn’t like spreadsheets or customer surveys. He’s not afraid to call himself authoritative. His time as one of the founders of Acne Studios, the major fashion house that started as a multidisciplinary studio, taught him that a company isn’t a “democratic organism. It needs a strong voice that can say yes or no.” It means, for example, that out of a hundred prototypes, Kouthoofd decides which one makes it to market, even if the team has calculated that it won’t sell. “We have a plastic PC case that you can build your own PC in. I wanted it to be $10,” he says. “Everyone said that was impossible because it cost $10 just to make. Then I said, ‘We won’t sell it, we’ll give it away for free. Now you don’t have an argument anymore.’” 

This kind of leadership can be tough to deal with. “It happens all the time,” says Yi-ying Hsieh, a Taiwan-born industrial designer who has been a core member of the design team for the past six years. “I spend weeks working on something, and then Jesper comes in, takes one look, and goes: ‘No, that’s ugly. Don’t do that.’ I’ve had to see a therapist because of it,” she adds, only half-joking. By now, she thinks her job is the best in the world. “teenage engineering is Jesper doing what he wants to do,” she says. “But we’re all okay with that because we want to contribute to what he wants to do.”

Although he’s a top-down leader, Kouthoofd is deeply involved in the day-to-day creative process. The early stages usually take place over lunch or an after-work beer. “I overhear someone saying, ‘Wouldn’t it be cool to have a unit like this?’” Kouthoofd says. “If it sounds interesting, I’ll run home straight away. I have a woodshop, 3D printers, a sewing machine — everything. I’ll make a model, bring it back to the office, and say, ‘Is this what you had in mind?’” 

To show me what happens in the next stages, Kouthoofd stands up from his chair and walks me through a door usually locked to visitors, marked with red-and-white “no entry” signs. Behind it, the space shifts from corporate office to something laboratory-like: wires and screwdrivers everywhere, machines humming, robots running functional tests, and young engineers and programmers working in concentrated silence, some at workbenches, others behind screens. “Some of this won’t be released for five to 10 years,” Kouthoofd says, pointing to a new project he believes will change our online life. 

Hsieh, searching for a way to capture teenage engineering’s typical way of working, offers a metaphor: “If you asked anyone before the invention of the car what they wanted, they would say: ‘I want a faster horse.’ They wouldn’t tell you they wanted a car because it didn’t exist yet. Other companies I’ve worked at try to make a faster horse. Jesper tries to make a car.” It fits Kouthoofd’s partly boyish, partly visionary ambition to create products that don’t answer a demand or solve a problem. “Otherwise, what’s the reward except money?” he says. “I want to make objects that comment on, or raise questions about, why we accept things as they are.”

That also applies to the OP-1 (and its successor, the OP-1 Field). Born in Kouthoofd’s garage, it’s used by artists as disparate as Aurora, Mike Dean, and Jean-Michel Jarre. Fifteen years after its launch, it remains one of the most sought-after instruments on Reverb, the world’s largest online marketplace for used music gear. Not bad for a pocket-size, battery-powered device Kouthoofd calls a protest against making music on laptops — less software-driven and serious, more intuitive and fun. More fundamentally, he says, it’s a rejection of the illusion that most synthesizer companies sell: “Ninety-nine percent of people who buy synths don’t use them as a productive tool for making music. It’s therapy. It’s entertainment. It’s a hobby. That’s what the OP-1 is. The first version didn’t even have an undo button.”   

“Think of it this way,” says Parisian musician and digital artist NSDOS, whose real name is Kirikoo Des. “Like an Apple device, some instruments think for you. The OP-1 is like Android or Linux: harder at first but also more free and creative, allowing you to put your own thinking into it.” Once he went down the rabbit hole of its workflow, the OP-1 became crucial to his experimental techno, which mixes organic sounds with industrial beats from custom-built hardware. 

He is far from alone: NSDOS is part of a global community of musicians, producers, and DJs formed around teenage engineering who use its gear everywhere from Berlin studios to Tokyo live sets. Lykke Li listens to her demos on a teenage engineering speaker while lying on the floor of her Los Angeles home. “It compresses [the audio] in a way that allows you to keep dreaming about what to add rather than freaking out over what’s not there,” she says. She cites the design as a draw, but also Kouthoofd himself and “how he thinks about things.” 

“It’s like one big family at this point,” she says. “I feel like teenage engineering is a point of view more than anything, and that’s what I resonate with the most.” 

The OP-1 has made teenage engineering what it is. Counterintuitive as it sounds, that’s precisely why leaving it behind is the most teenage engineering thing Kouthoofd could do. He doesn’t want the company to be pigeonholed as a producer of synthesizers. In fact, he doesn’t want it to be defined by any single product at all. 

For Kouthoofd, teenage engineering is its own most important creation. “We shouldn’t make profits out of the products,” he says. “The real value lies in the company as a whole.” He no longer wants ideas to take the form of “obvious end products” — like, say, another synthesizer. 

More simply, he wants teenage engineering to be a place where people never get bored. “What’s the point of going to work,” he asks, “if it isn’t fun?”

cachedArticles.title: Legendary Makeup Artist Bobbi Brown Is Still Doing Makeup Her Way
cachedArticles.author: Elizabeth Denton
cachedArticles.snippet: The Jones Road Beauty founder talks viral complexion products, building a brand in the age of TikTok and why mascara is never going away.
cachedArticles.content:
Bobbi Brown has spent decades shaping the way we think about makeup. After building her namesake beauty brand into an industry powerhouse (and leaving the company in the hands of Estée Lauder in 2016), the legendary makeup artist returned to the business in 2020 with Jones Road Beauty. The line is built around her longstanding philosophy that makeup should make you look like yourself, only better. (She’s anti-contour for a reason.)

In the last six years, Brown has expanded the brand into solid range of easy-to-use, multi-purpose products, some of which have gone TikTok-viral (including What the Foundation and Miracle Balm). Jones Road Beauty also bet big on brick-and-mortar; there are 18 store locations, with 20 total expected by the end of 2026.

We caught up with Brown at her newest location in Santa Monica, CA, where she was hosting a community masterclass with her latest launches, Wide Awake Brightening Concealer and Neutralizer. Below, she discusses her aversion to trends, advice for beauty founders and thoughts on Sephora tweens.

What are Jones Road Beauty’s top products right now?

The first five or six are complexion products. I’m not surprised. It’s What the Foundation, Miracle Balm, our Face Pencils, Just Enough Tinted Moisturizer and our Foundation Stick.

What’s special about Wide Awake Brightening Concealer?

It really does cover but it feels like you have nothing on. It has an eight-hour wear claim, it doesn’t crease and it really covers dark circles. And if you don’t know what a neutralizer is, it’s a color — pink or peach — that gets rid of darkness because some people have purple, some have green, some have brown, some even have white under their eyes. You neutralize it first and then you lighten it up with a concealer and you look wide awake.

With the beauty landscape changing so quickly, how do you keep a brand relevant?

My philosophy is: do what is right, do what you believe in and don’t chase trends. I know there was a trend that mascara is out. Mascara’s not out.

View this post on Instagram

What’s different about building a brand now vs in the 1990s?

There’s so much different about building a brand the second time around, especially in 2026. First of all, social media is your friend. It is a great way to know what’s happening. It’s a great way to tell people what’s happening and it doesn’t cost a lot of money. You just talk into the camera and you tell people the truth.

What’s your advice to new founders?

You already founded a company; just calm down. Just breathe. And just really know that it takes time to learn the business, to learn what works, to learn what doesn’t; and if things don’t work for a second, don’t panic. Take a break and really think about what you could have done better and what you can do now.

You’re also an author of teen beauty books. What do you think about teen beauty today?

Every decade, things change. I’ve written two books for teenage girls and it’s amazing when you go into one of the stores, especially Sephora and Ulta, and you see these 10- and 11-year-old kids with their dads on a weekend, which is really adorable, coming to look for the next retinol cream. I didn’t know what a retinol cream was. I still don’t know what a retinol cream is! I think there are good things and bad things about everything and as long as you’re focused on the right things — taking care of yourself, being nice to people — that’s the advice you give to teens.

What’s your beauty industry hot take?

There are so many brands out there. Do your homework. Know what you like. And by the way, don’t [let] anyone force you to buy anything you don’t want to.

cachedArticles.content:
These are the stories making headlines in fashion on Tuesday.

Marc Jacobs’ Post-LVMH Plan

Marc Jacobs’ namesake label is beginning a new chapter under WHP Global and G-III Apparel Group, which acquired it from LVMH this year. G-III CEO Morris Goldfarb has pledged to preserve the runway shows and the Spring Street headquarters, while setting a goal of lifting the handbag-heavy business to $1 billion in sales. Though, some full-price stores could be shuttered. Jacobs, who has about two years left on his contract, hopes the partnership will be built on mutual respect and will revive a lower-priced ready-to-wear line. {Business of Fashion/paywalled}

Why Bootleg Merch Is Thriving

Unlicensed Harry Styles and Knicks apparel is selling on New York streets, where vendors outside Madison Square Garden and other venues charge far less than official merchandise, which can cost $50 to $85 a piece. High licensing costs and bland official designs have opened a door for knockoffs to fill the gap. Fans often buy both, picking up an official souvenir at a pop-up or concert and a cheaper, more creative bootleg on the way out. {Vogue Business/paywalled}

L’Oréal Hires Restructuring Advisers Over Talc-Related Claims

L’Oréal’s U.S. unit has hired restructuring advisers Weil Gotshal & Manges and Ducera Partners to explore ways to handle mounting U.S. legal liabilities tied to talc and other chemical ingredients used in some of its products. One option under review would move the tort liabilities into a separate entity and sell it to an outside investor. This would allow L’Oréal to transfer responsibility for the claims to a new owner. {Wall Street Journal/paywalled)

Norway Moves to Restrict Smart Glasses in Public

Norway’s government plans to introduce a temporary ban on camera-equipped smart glasses in public venues such as parks, beaches, museums, schools and gyms, though private use would still be allowed. The minority Labour government needs support from other parties to pass the bill, and it has also tasked an expert group with drafting permanent rules. “I am worried that new, powerful technology is being introduced where people risk being photographed, filmed or audio-recorded without knowing it,” Digitalization and Public Governance Minister Torgeir Micaelsen said in a statement. {Reuters/paywalled}

Swedish Stockings Eyes U.S. Growth

Swedish Stockings is stepping up its U.S. push with its first American pop-up in New York, running from Oct. 7 through Oct. 18. At its pop-up, it will pre-launch two new versions of its $65 Roxana Tiger Tights, co-designed with Leandra Medine Cohen. Listen to the full conversation between Popflex Founder, CEO and Head Designer Cassey Ho and Fashionista Associate Editor Catie Pusateri on The Fashionista Network on Spotify.

https://open.spotify.com/episode/0FcRBgIOIz4h0KbvIzHNOR?si=GRybNfISSBG1wpG_i7YleA

While preparing to graduate with a degree in pre-med biology, Cassey Ho taught Pilates on the side and started a YouTube channel for her students called Blogilates in 2009. After unintentionally tapping into an online audience beyond her real-life students (Blogilates now boasts more than 11 million YouTube subscribers), Ho began designing her own activewear pieces to wear in her videos, and officially launched her label Popflex in 2016. A decade later, Popflex is one of the leading activewear brands in the space, known for viral designs like its Cloud Hoodie and Pirouette Skort.

In 2023, Shein took notice and duped Popflex’s Pirouette Skort, a sheer tiered skirt concealing inner shorts. In response, Ho successfully patented her design. Just over a year later, Taylor Swift wore the Popflex skort in her “I Can Do It With A Broken Heart” music video; it sold out “in a matter of minutes,” according to Ho. With the patent, Ho was now able to protect the design against fast-fashion dupes that often arise when a product goes viral.

“If I don’t fight to protect my design, people are just going to walk all over me,” Ho said during our conversation. “So it’s a lot of emotional energy to deal with this, but at the same time, by fighting for my design, I also speak up for other independent designers who may not have the platform to speak about these things that happen all the time, unfortunately.”

On The Fashionista Network, Ho also discussed solving for common activewear woes in her designs, testing Popflex’s sizing guide on real consumers, launching Blogilates for Target in 2025, repurposing fast-fashion dupes of her designs and more. Watch the full interview on YouTube below.

Virginie Viard Reflects on Being Fired From Chanel

In her new book, “Un Regard: Une Vie Chez Chanel” (loosely translated to “My Life at Chanel”), Virginie Viard opened up about the emotional aftermath of being unexpectedly fired as Chanel’s creative director. She wrote that she was caught off guard by the sudden dismissal and was hurt that the company implied her work was unremarkable. She also suggested she received harsher criticism than her male peers. She also discussed balancing her responsibilities at Miu Miu and Prada, what she wants to be remembered for, the importance of living in the present and how she handles running an ultra-luxury brand while the world faces poverty and war. {Business of Fashion/paywalled}

cachedArticles.title: Djerf Avenue Finds Its First Permanent Home in New York City With SoHo Flagship
cachedArticles.author: Hannah Malach
cachedArticles.snippet: Founder Matilda Djerf's viral clothing and lifestyle brand is officially putting down roots.
cachedArticles.content:
Three years after opening her brand’s first pop-up in New York City, Matilda Djerf’s Djerf Avenue is back in the Big Apple for good. The Scandi label has permanently settled in SoHo at 25 Bond St., just down the block from Gwyneth Paltrow’s Goop and Gigi Hadid’s Guest in Residence.

“We didn’t do a lot of research about the best city to do the first store in,” Djerf tells Fashionista of the new flagship. “It’s always about the gut feeling, and New York is such a special place for us.”

The 29-year-old Swedish influencer, who launched Djerf Avenue with her fiancé Rasmus Johansson in 2019, cites community events such as the brand’s Guggenheim fashion show as an inflection point for her company, which did $36 million in sales in 2024.

Although a workplace harassment scandal threatened to throttle Djerf’s momentum, she managed to soften the blow by addressing the allegations — including claims of “bullying” and a “degrading” work environment — head-on. Acknowledging her shortcomings in a public apology, as well as a series of interviews, Djerf chalked it up to being a young, inexperienced first-time founder. Plus, Djerf Avenue’s rapid pace of growth made it challenging to scale.

With the appointment of seasoned retail consultant Nanna Hedlund as interim chief executive officer in 2025, the company promptly expanded its human resources department and created a work environment task force, allowing employees to submit anonymous surveys as feedback. Hedlund stepped down as interim CEO in February 2026 and now sits on Djerf Avenue’s board.

Djerf bounced back with a successful Selfridges pop-up in London a year after the exposé. Within hours of opening, Djerf Avenue purchases made up 70% of the floor’s sales, outpacing even Kim Kardashian’s Skims.

Perhaps it’s a testament to the quality of Djerf’s products, which are produced in Europe (Portugal, Italy and Sweden, to be exact) and available in sizes XXS to 3XL at a mid-range price point. She successfully expanded the brand beyond clothing and accessories, introducing homeware and beauty products that bolster Djerf Avenue’s mission to serve as a “big sister” to its customers.

This thread also runs through the new NYC boutique, which Djerf said is staffed with employees familiar with the sizing, fit and fabrication of each item.

“As a consumer myself — I’ve shopped in so many stores — the level of expertise [among sales associates] can look very different,” Djerf explains. “Sometimes you walk into a store and you don’t really feel welcome. That’s something we absolutely do not want, and it’s something we learned very quickly with our pop-ups. I wanted to bring Scandinavia to New York but I don’t want it to feel so cold and minimalistic that you’re scared to sit on the couch.”

The layout of the store, rendered with help from LEAP Architecture, was primarily designed by Djerf herself and takes inspiration from her island summer home in Sweden. (Think warm woods, lots of natural light and high ceilings.) The shop is also decked out in the brand’s best-selling hand-painted prints in the form of decorative drapery and upholstery.

The boutique is stocked with pieces Djerf Avenue fans know and love, such as its best-selling line of Go Slow pajamas and ready-to-wear staples like the Weekend Blazer. Shoppers will also be treated to a selection of in-store exclusives, including playing cards, reusable water bottles and yellow cab keychains.

Teaming up with local vendors was an integral part of Djerf Avenue’s pop-up strategy, a tradition that the new store is upholding. For opening weekend, Leon’s Bagels and Bluestone Lane returned to serve up strawberry bagels and matcha (a nod to the brand’s popular Summer Berries collection). Such collaborations are expected to be a consistent feature of the flagship.

With brick-and-mortar retail and in-person brand experiences on the upswing, now felt like the perfect time to start building out Djerf Avenue’s physical footprint. What’s more, the label’s typical customer purchases a higher quantity of items in-person as opposed to when shopping virtually.

“You get so much information from the customer that is incredibly important for growing the business and evolving as a business owner,” Djerf said of operating a standalone boutique. “When people try things on, you can stand in the store and immediately hear their first reaction. That’s something you can’t get when they purchase online.”

The Djerf Avenue flagship is now open at 25 Bond St. in New York City, Monday through Saturday from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. and Sunday from 12 p.m. to 6 p.m.
