These are the stories making headlines in fashion on Friday.

Nike Cuts Jobs Under New ‘Pace’ Restructuring Plan

On Thursday, Nike announced a restructuring plan called “Pace” that will cut jobs next year and consolidate its four geographic regions into three, after quarterly sales fell 4% to $11.2 billion. The company expects the plan to save $2.5 billion by fiscal 2031 at an implementation cost of $1 billion, including $300 million in severance. Sales in Greater China dropped 22% — the fifth straight quarterly decline in the region. Nike expects full-year revenue to fall by a high-single-digit percentage. {Nike; Business of Fashion/paywalled}

Sycamore Close to Selling Boots for $9 Billion

Sycamore Partners, the private equity firm that took control of Boots by acquiring its parent company Walgreens Boots Alliance Inc. in 2025, is nearing a deal to sell the chain to the Canadian Weston family. The sale would hand over more than 1,800 U.K. stores just weeks after new CEO Alex Baldock started and would end speculation about a London IPO. Boots reported revenue of £7.5 billion ($9.9 billion) in its latest year’s accounts, up 3.2%. {Business of Fashion/paywalled}

ChatGPT Adds Virtual Try-On to Its Features

OpenAI updated ChatGPT Images to version 2.5, adding a virtual try-on feature and a way for shoppers to save items they like in a personal library. Users can upload a selfie and tap “try on” in shopping results, or upload a photo of a style they want to see on themselves. {WWD/paywalled}

How the Target Boycott Impacted Black Beauty Founders

In January, consumers began boycotting Target over its rollback of diversity, equity and inclusion programs. Since then, the retailer has not restored the programs. Sales and traffic have rebounded from the initial slump, but Black-owned brands that rely on Target shelf space may have taken the hardest hit, according to several beauty founders and executives. The debate has been sharpened by the launch of Target Beauty Studio, where only two of 90 brands are Black-owned or Black-founded. {Beauty Independent/paywalled}

Business of Fashion Unveils the BoF 500 Class of 2026

The Business of Fashion unveiled The BoF 500 Class of 2026, adding 100 people to its index of figures shaping the global fashion industry and bringing the total to 1,713 members. Among the new class are designers Dario Vitale and Foday Dumbuya, executives Luca De Meo of Kering and Hillary Super of Victoria’s Secret as well as athletes and entertainers Eileen Gu, Naomi Osaka and Teyana Taylor. All of these new entrants will be honored at a gala at the Shangri-La Paris on Saturday. {Fashionista inbox}

What’s the opposite of gatekeeping? Welcome to “Payment Processing,” in which we ask stylish, generally cool people who’ve tried it all about their favorite fashion and beauty buys.

When someone tells me they aren’t familiar with Mckenna Grace, I tell them they probably are, no matter what generation they’re from. The 20-year-old has been a working actor for 14 years. She’s perhaps best known for playing young Tonya Harding in “I, Tonya,” her Emmy-nominated stint in “The Handmaid’s Tale” and her roles in two “Ghostbusters” movies. In 2025, she starred alongside her real-life boyfriend, Mason Thames, in “Regretting You,” a film adaptation of Colleen Hoover’s novel, on which she also served as an executive producer.

View this post on Instagram

And she’s not slowing down. Grace has a handful of buzzy films slated through early 2027 (notably, for this interview: “Scooby-Doo: Origins”), as well as new music; plus, she’s currently the face of Crocs’ cozy fall/winter campaign.

We caught up with Grace on a Crocs set in Los Angeles to chat about her favorite luxury lip oils, drugstore makeup finds and her dreams of having Adéla-pink hair.

What’s a luxury beauty item you’re into right now? Why?

I like the little Dior lip oils, especially because they’ve come out with a lot of purple stuff lately. I’m very much in my purple vibes lately. That’s my era. So I like the Dior purple blushes and their lip oils.

What’s a drugstore/mass market beauty item you love?

Any sort of eyeliner. I especially like getting a nude or a white that I can put on my waterline. I heard somewhere that it makes your eyes pop. But also, I saw it on TikTok actually, I love the L’Oréal Paris Telescopic Mascara.

What’s an accessory you’re eyeing right now?

I’m trying to get more in my sunglasses game… I’ve been looking for any sort of purple sunglasses or things like that, but I’ve loved Miu Miu’s sunglasses lately. I think that they’re really pretty.

What shoes do you want to buy right now?

I walked in and I saw [the Crocs Chalet Clogs] today. They’re so cute with the little ribbons. I feel like it’d be really cute to wear these and get a ribbon that looks like that and put it in my hair.

What’s a fall fashion must-have you swear by?

I love cozy socks. I love knitted knee-high. Right now I’m wearing the sheer one that goes with my Crocs. I love a little grandpa sweater moment. Any sort of cozy thing: a scarf, a sweater, knee-highs.

Have you been influenced by a celeb or influencer recently?

Between Adéla, and there’s this influencer that I really like, I think her name is Miranda Ray. She always has really colorful hair and she’ll pop up on my For You Page every once in a while. It’s making me want to have pink hair, but I don’t think my job would like that. It’s not a product or anything, but I feel like I really want pink or colorful hair.

Of all the characters you’ve played, which one’s wardrobe did you love the most?

I definitely loved [Scooby-Doo’s] Daphne Blake’s wardrobe, and I feel like that’s pretty self-explanatory. Everything in my life is slowly becoming purple. I definitely maybe stole a few items. I did steal a lot of my wardrobe from “Regretting You” because it was really cute, easy, everyday items. And coincidentally, that was Erinn [Knight], who was our costume designer on “Regretting You,” [and] was our costume designer on “Scooby.” So that makes sense as to why I loved both of those characters’ wardrobes.

cachedArticles.title: This Italian Jewelry House's Milan Atelier Is Hidden in Plain Sight
cachedArticles.author: Catie Pusateri
cachedArticles.snippet: Founded by gemologists Milena Bernocco and her son Nicolas Garatti, the maison currently owns 60% of the world's known green diamonds.
cachedArticles.content:
Just off one of Milan’s bustling streets lies an unmarked, gemstone-shaped door etched into an otherwise unassuming wall. To passersby, it’s merely another work of art steps from the Castello Sforzesco, but to a select few, it’s the entrance to Garatti‘s high jewelry atelier. Its hidden-in-plain-sight doorway feels closer to a plot point in a thrilling mystery novel rather than a real-life showroom, especially once visitors bypass a second layer of security and enter a sparkling display of diamonds. (And don’t bother trying to look Garatti up on Google Maps — it’s intentionally off-the-grid.)

Founded in 2018 by Milena Bernocco and her son Nicolas Garatti, the Italian high jewelry house specializes in green diamonds. You’ve likely heard of their yellow or blue counterparts (see: the Tiffany Diamond or the Hope Diamond), but what, you may ask, are green diamonds? The rare gemstone’s greenish hue comes from natural exposure to radiation over millennia, resulting in various levels of saturation and clarity. (No, they’re not radioactive; I asked.)

In fact, any colored diamonds are exceedingly rare, as only one out of 10,000 carats of fashioned diamonds displays “fancy color,” according to the Gemological Institute of America (GIA), a nonprofit organization and the global authority on diamonds, colored stones and pearls. But green diamonds rank among the rarest of the rare, second only to red diamonds. Now, Garatti is further positioning itself as the premier destination for the green-tinted gems: It currently owns 60% of the world’s known green diamonds as well as more than 90% of those currently available on the market, per the maison.

For Bernocco, a career gemologist, two factors fueled her decision to go all-in on green diamonds. “The first is the sheer beauty of their color: a magnetic green born from a long, natural process of formation,” she told Fashionista over email, translated from Italian. “The second is our desire to bring these gems the recognition they deserve for their rarity and allure, as they represent the second rarest diamond color in the world.”

View the 2 images of this gallery on the original article

Inside its Milan atelier, Garatti artisans combine traditional Italian craftsmanship with contemporary design to create custom pieces. Bernocco spearheads the design process for each of the label’s capsules, including its Settecento collection (a multi-strand necklace referencing 1700s high jewelry) and its Venezia collection (statement earrings and a necklace inspired by Venetian chandeliers). Unlike many of the industry’s front-facing high jewelry players — Cartier, Van Cleef & Arpels and Tiffany & Co., for example — Garatti firmly commits to its custom, made-to-order business model.

“What sets our brand apart from competitors is the sheer uniqueness of our creations,” Bernocco shared. “We craft exclusively one-of-a-kind pieces, tailored ad hoc for each client, alongside museum-grade collections featured on the world’s most prestigious red carpets.”

As one of its most notable celebrity placements, Garatti’s green diamonds (more than 41 carats of them, worth a whopping $35 million, to be exact), graced the neck of Kate Hudson at the 98th Academy Awards in 2026. Other A-listers like Angelina Jolie, Emma Stone, Gwyneth Paltrow, Penélope Cruz and Lupita Nyong’o have also donned the Italian house’s rare jewels.

Regardless of a prospective client’s means, the atelier’s concealed entryway ensures that not just anyone can waltz in and purchase a multimillion-dollar diamond necklace. Instead, Garatti operates on an invitation-only basis. “The selection of our clientele extends beyond financial standing — even though our creations represent true luxury — and is rooted primarily in moral and ethical values that align with our brand identity,” Bernocco explained. “Our ideal client is a person of refined culture, a passionate patron of the arts and actively engaged in social and humanitarian causes.”

This emphasis on ethical values and transparency continues into Garatti’s diamond sourcing, as the jewelry house uses the Kimberley Process (KP), which is an international initiative established in 2000 to eradicate conflict diamonds from the legitimate trade. According to KP, conflict diamonds are “rough diamonds used by rebel movements or their allies to finance conflict aimed at undermining legitimate governments.” Plus, each Garatti diamond is guaranteed and certified by the GIA. (Translation: No “blood diamonds” here, per the company.)

Despite many high jewelry brands targeting female consumers with glittering necklaces and dangling earrings, the wider gemology industry is largely run by men. While scaling the ranks in her gemology career, Bernocco eventually hit a wall. So, after deciding to go out on her own, she brought in her eldest son Nicolas (along with her younger son Luca) to help open more doors.

“It was by no means an easy journey, but my passion and determination to open up this world to true connoisseurs are what [have] driven me to build our brand,” she said. “From a young age, my son Nicolas — now president of Garatti — supported me in its founding, standing by my side to navigate the challenges and obstacles of this industry.” Though in Bernocco’s opinion, “this kind of art is even more beautiful and better with a feminine vision.”

In an age when lab-grown diamonds are becoming increasingly popular on the jewelry market, Garatti highlights its green diamonds’ exclusivity, permanence and exceptional rarity as its key differentiation points. As the high jewelry maison looks to the future, Garatti is focusing on preserving its time-honored craftsmanship for a new generation. (In fact, one of its in-house artisans is a 19-year-old woman, sitting alongside male colleagues with decades of experience.) 

“As a brand, we are dedicated to educating and inspiring anyone who encounters our world, ensuring that the passion and love for this fine art endure through time,” Bernocco said.

cachedArticles.snippet: Retail placement was once viewed as the ultimate sign of success. Now, stricter margins, inventory requirements and performance expectations are forcing beauty brands to reconsider what it takes to survive on the shelf.
cachedArticles.content:
For years, getting into a major beauty retailer was treated as the ultimate marker of legitimacy for emerging brands in the industry. A Sephora, Ulta Beauty or national mass-market launch could transform an emerging label into an industry success story almost overnight. Today, the prestige of that placement remains in many ways, but the impact of it has changed.

A prominent retail partnership is no longer a finish line; rather, it’s a starting point, a high-stakes test of whether a brand can finance inventory, absorb tighter margins, satisfy compliance requirements, fund marketing and keep customers coming back once launch-day excitement fades.

Retailers want more than a strong product. They also expect differentiation, an engaged community, reliable fulfillment and a plan for sustained sell-through. Brands, meanwhile, must determine whether the exposure is worth the cash, control and capacity the partnership demands.

What “Retail-Ready” Means Now

“Retail-ready isn’t just having a great product anymore. It’s having a business that’s ready to be put under a microscope,” says Kate Souied, head of marketing at FlutterHabit, which recently entered Sephora. “Retail doesn’t fix your business; it puts it on full display.”

That scrutiny begins before the first purchase order.

Jessica Phillips, vice president of merchandising at Ulta Beauty, says the retailer looks for brands with differentiated innovation, compelling storytelling and an operational foundation capable of translating an existing consumer connection into retail. “Being retail-ready today means much more than having a great product,” she says. “The strongest brands have begun building an engaged community and have the operational foundation and long-term vision to translate that connection into retail.”

Credo Beauty Co-Founder and CEO Annie Jackson starts with an even more basic requirement: a strategy. “‘I’ll take a PO [purchase order] from anyone’ is not a strategy,” she says. A brand should understand which retail partners serve its positioning and can add growth without taking business away from the channels it has already built, Jackson explains. Credo launches only 12 to 15 brands a year, and a clear point of difference is the most persuasive sign of readiness.

At Ulta, success is measured through sales as well as whether a brand attracts new shoppers, encourages repeat engagement and remains relevant across the retailer’s omnichannel ecosystem. For Credo, the calculation is more direct.

Beyond sales, Jackson says, success is rarely measured by anything other than productivity per unit of shelf space. “We can’t afford to run a store like it’s a museum,” she says, pointing to the fixed costs and thin margins associated with physical retail.

Related: How Beauty Became Obsessed With Bold, Expressive Packaging

The Cost of Getting on the Shelf

For founders, the celebratory retail partnership launch announcement can obscure the less glamorous question underneath it: Can the business afford to succeed at said retailer?

Veronica Pedersen, founder of Timeless Skin Care, asked precisely that before expanding into more than 1,500 Target stores. The company estimated how much product it would need, secured raw materials and packaging components and assessed its production capacity for both the initial order and rapid replenishment if the products took off. Its in-house manufacturing gives the brand direct control over quality and production, but the rollout still required systems for purchase-order processing, electronic data interchange and vendor compliance.

“One of the biggest misconceptions is that a purchase order is the same thing as profitability. It is not,” Pedersen tells Fashionista.

Before saying yes to national distribution, founders must determine whether they can finance inventory, support marketing, absorb payment terms and meet increased demand without weakening the rest of the company. Timeless forecasts 12 to 24 months out across direct-to-consumer, Amazon, national retail and international distribution.

Liz Folce, founder and CEO of Nakery Beauty, has observed the same shift over more than 30 years in the beauty industry. Retailers can quickly see what is selling, converting and driving repeat purchases, leaving brands with less time to find their footing.

“You’re not handing a retailer your product and expecting them to build the business for you,” she says. “You need to come with inventory, marketing support, content, sampling, education and a plan to drive the customer to that retailer.”

Those needs create a long list of expenses. Inventory is financed ahead of payment. Packaging may need to change. Then come displays, testers, samples, freight, retailer programs, advertising, education, customer support, potential deductions and additional staffing. If an item sells faster than expected, the company needs more product and working capital immediately. If it moves slowly, cash remains trapped in inventory.

Souied puts the first requirement more plainly: “Cash,” she jokes. “Seriously though, retail is expensive before you ever make a dollar back.”

Building the Retail Engine

That transformation became clear for hair- and scalp-care brand Nutrire while preparing to launch at Ulta through the retailer’s Sparked program. General Manager Kristen Chase says the company was not originally built for wholesale, so preparing for national retail required it to rework its forecasting, inventory planning and fulfillment while developing a trade-marketing capability.

“[P]reparing for Ulta meant rewiring a big part of our operation,” Chase says. “Selling direct to a guest and supplying a national retailer are two different disciplines.”

Nutrire invested in clinical testing, packaging, creator relationships and consumer education while keeping its internal team lean. It also brought all nine products in its scalp-to-strand system to Ulta rather than fragmenting the assortment.

By the end of the process, Chase says, the team understood that retail readiness was less about preparing for a single launch and more about building an engine capable of performing week after week.

Related: Is Private Equity’s Involvement in Beauty Stifling Brand Individuality?

Every Retailer Has Its Own Playbook

Every channel and each retailer demands a different version of retail readiness. While there is of course plenty of overlap, what works for one may not necessarily be true for another.

Folce says Nakery approaches Ulta, Amazon and HSN as separate environments: Ulta depends on physical and digital discovery, packaging, positioning and education. Amazon rewards search visibility, reviews, advertising and conversion. HSN relies more heavily on storytelling and product demonstration.

Timeless, menawhile, takes a similar approach across its retail partners Target, Amazon, Nordstrom and Macy’s. Not every product belongs in every channel, Pedersen says, and more distribution does not automatically equal better distribution.

Ryan Siegel, co-founder of beauty-hydration brand H2Glow, prioritizes audience alignment, data transparency, pricing protection and commercial terms over a retailer’s size.

“A smaller partner with the right audience always outperforms a massive retailer where your core customer isn’t looking,” he says.

The question is not simply whether a retailer will accept a brand, but whether the partnership will strengthen the business. Jackson advises brands to ask retailers for explicit sales expectations and a clear definition of what could lead to discontinuation. Waiting until performance slips to discuss a turnaround may be too late.

Access to the merchant matters, too. Jackson notes that one merchant may oversee 20 or more brands, so founders should determine whether they will be able to discuss the business at least monthly. Brands should also understand the cost of samples, gratis, co-op marketing and field coverage.

What Retailers Bring to the Partnership

Retailers say they are trying to help emerging brands close some of these gaps. Phillips points to Ulta’s MUSE Accelerator, which has supported more than 32 emerging brands with more than $1.5 million in funding and over 150 hours of coaching since 2022. Ulta can also connect partners with third-party logistics providers and offer customized merchandising, digital storytelling, education and in-store experiences.

“Supporting emerging brands goes far beyond providing shelf space,” Phillips says. “We think about how we can support founders at different stages of their journey and help build businesses positioned for long-term success.”

Chase says Ulta’s support of Nutrire exceeded her expectations, while Phlur Chief Marketing Officer Erica Dunivan credits Sephora with helping the fragrance brand expand from the U.S. and Canada into the Middle East, Mexico and Europe. “Sephora is a true brand growth partner,” she says. “They have a deep understanding of Phlur and our point of difference.”

Those examples show what a productive partnership can unlock: scale, credibility, new markets and consumer discovery that would be difficult for an emerging brand to build alone.

Sell-Through Is the Real Finish Line

The danger arrives when scale becomes the strategy. A crowded shelf can pressure brands to adapt their assortments, packaging or messaging in ways that make them easier to merchandise, but harder to distinguish.

The sources Fashionista consulted for his story draw their boundaries in different places. Siegel considers pack configurations and promotional timing flexible, but calls H2Glow’s pricing integrity and narrative “sacred.” Folce will change Nakery’s assortment by retailer, but not its focus on women over 50. Dunivan says Phlur adjusts campaigns for local markets while keeping its fragrance storytelling consistent.

Even with the right partner, placement does not create demand on its own. Phillips says the biggest misconception founders hold is that getting onto the shelf is the finish line. “In many ways, that’s when the work really begins,” she says.

Souied is sharper: “Shelf space is an opportunity, not a marketing strategy.”

That reframing changes the metric that matters. Door count may make an impressive press release, but velocity reveals whether the business is working.

“Getting in is not the win, but selling through is,” Siegel says. “Watch how fast the product moves per store, not how many stores you are in.”

Major retail can still be transformative. But the new definition of readiness asks brands to prove much of what retail once promised to create: consumer awareness, community, operational maturity and a reason to believe the business will last.

The shelf is not a trophy. It is a weekly performance review, and the brands most likely to survive it are the ones willing to ask not only “Can we get in?” but “Should we, and can we afford what happens next?”

These are the stories making headlines in fashion on Thursday.

Jay-Z’s MarcyPen Capital Partners May Acquire 50% Stake in Fenty Beauty

MarcyPen Capital Partners — an investment platform co-founded by Jay-Z, D’Rita and Robbie Robinson — may acquire a 50% stake in Rihanna’s Fenty Beauty from LVMH, Puck reported on Wednesday. The transaction could be signed within the next three to four weeks. Terms of the deal were not disclosed. Since its successful 2017 launch, Fenty Beauty has been in decline for several years as competition in the celebrity-founded beauty brand space grows. {Puck/paywalled}

How Emerging Designers Approach Celebrity Placements

While celebrity placements earn emerging designers notoriety early on in their careers, it can also be difficult for rising brand founders to stay on top of the fast-paced celebrity style news cycle. Emerging designers need to carefully select which stars reflect their established brand aesthetic. Capacity is limited for small designers to fulfill celebrity requests, but the right moment can pay off in sales: When Dua Lipa wore a Julie Kegels look last year, the designer said it sold out on the brand’s site “in a second”. {Vogue Business/paywalled}

Apple Martin Makes Runway Debut at Chloé

Apple Martin, the daughter of Gywneth Paltrow and Chris Martin, made her runway debut at Chloé’s Spring 2027 show in Paris on Thursday. Martin previously appeared in Chloé’s À La Plage campaign earlier this summer, so walking in the brand’s show was an expected next step. {Dazed}

Telfar to Host Its Largest Sample Sale Yet

Telfar is hosting a sample sale from Tuesday, Oct. 6 through Sunday, Oct. 11 at 1 Hanson Place in Brooklyn. More than 30,000 garments and bags will be priced at up to 90% off. The label is also launching Bag Redemption, a program allowing customers to bring in their existing Telfar bags (regardless of age or condition) and redeem them toward a new bag or wardrobe. Doors open at 10 a.m. on Oct. 6. At 11 a.m., guests will be part of Telfar’s 2027 Paris Runway presentation with hosts and a surprise performance. {Fashionista inbox}

Levi Strauss & Co. Names New CFO

Levi Strauss & Co. has named John Vandemore its executive vice president and chief financial officer, effective Nov. 1, 2026. Vandemore joins from Skechers U.S.A., Inc., where he served as CFO for the past nine years. He succeeds Harmit Singh, who announced his retirement from his role as executive vice president and chief financial & growth officer in April. {Levi Strauss & Co.}

Patek Philippe to Remain Independent, Owner Says

Luxury watch manufacturer Patek Philippe is not for sale, according to owner and president Thierry Stern. He said he plans to hand the multi-billion dollar business to his two sons, though he did not specify when. Stern noted that his “target is to stay independent,” as his family has owned the company since 1932. {Business of Fashion/paywalled}

cachedArticles.title: How To Make It as a Fashion Photographer
cachedArticles.author: Erica Jean
cachedArticles.snippet: "For me, tenacity, kindness and a healthy amount of delusion have gone a surprisingly long way."
cachedArticles.content:
Fashion photography — a space defined by glossy magazine covers, dreamy advertising campaigns and designer-filled editorials — has never required a formal degree. (Just look to Steven Meisel’s storied photography career, achieved with only a background in fashion illustration from Parsons.) In an age when a camera sits in everyone’s pocket, and an Instagram post can get more traction than a magazine spread, the field is more saturated than ever. Now, getting into the industry is no longer the hard part — standing out is.

Ahead, Fashionista asked four fashion photographers what it really takes to make it in this competitive field.

You Don’t Need Credentials or the ‘Right’ Gear

Lyrie Wang, whose work has appeared in Harper’s Bazaar and Esquire, had a camera and a dream when she quit her job as a product manager in tech to pursue fashion photography. All she knew was how to take cute pictures for Instagram and curate an aesthetic feed.

To learn the basics, she turned to YouTube, looking up what “aperture” and “shutter speed” mean and watching tutorials on how to color grade and adjust her camera settings. “That’s the easy part. The information is there,” Wang explains. Thalía Gochez — a Los Angeles-born photographer snapshotting BIPOC subjects across the world — did the same, using YouTube to learn how to load film.

There aren’t hard and fast rules around gear, either. Dan Bassini, a street style photographer, exclusively uses a 35-millimeter point-and-shoot. “People don’t take it seriously, which I use to my benefit because they don’t think I’m a professional photographer,” he shares. “So I can get in places that other people with a big camera rig can’t.”

Gochez bought her first camera for a dollar at a San Francisco flea market. Years later, she captured a Nike campaign on that same camera, battery cover missing and held together with tape.

Just Go for It

Despite hailing from very different backgrounds, all four photographers we spoke with say one trait is essential: the audacity to act. “You have to be unapologetic about putting yourself forward,” London-based fashion photographer Emily White says.

“I am shameless about overselling myself,” Wang echoes. With no prior experience under her belt, she posted in a Facebook group for photographers and models, introducing herself as a photographer who was looking to shoot.

For Gochez, this audacity surfaced in a community college fashion styling class, when she was watching a photographer work but felt the urge to take the camera and try it herself. “If he’s figured out that camera, I can figure it out,” she says. “Like, what makes him different from me?”

Bassini’s audacity takes shape in simply showing up: Without an invite, he’s photographed New York Fashion Week for a decade. “‘What if I just try to walk through the front door?'” he recalls asking himself. “It works more than you’d expect.” This September, Bassini unveiled his 10-year retrospective titled “No Invite,” which featured photographic highlights of sneaking into NYFW parties and standing outside runway venues.

Manage the Fear

That’s not to say a photographer’s career is easy (or glamorous). “I definitely had nerves and moments of doubt (still do), but I never really let them stop me,” White shares. Pushing through that discomfort has allowed her to eventually build a portfolio that includes Cartier, Dior Beauty and Hypebeast.

For Gochez, having imposter syndrome is inevitable, even part of the process. “You’re gonna feel all these emotions, but you have to understand that’s part of the creative process, and you have to see it through towards the end,” she explains.

On the other hand, for Wang, splitting everything into small, manageable steps meant she never felt like she was taking a big leap. “The first step is really all you need to get the ball rolling, and then every other step becomes more clear as you go,” she shares.

Develop a Point of View

To stand out, each photographer developed a distinct signature, and many found their inspiration from their own lives. Gochez started by photographing girls from her own neighborhood: girls the industry didn’t consider models, but whom Gochez found beautiful. That perspective became her signature: photographing people of color.

“I was relentless in discovering my artistic voice and it being so distinctively ‘me’ meant that the industry couldn’t ignore that,” she says. Her clients include Vogue, The New York Times and Apple.

Bassini, too, drew from his life. He got his start in music photography — a scrappy, DIY scene — so he brought that approach to the glamorous world of fashion week. In practice, that meant capturing close-up portraits while other photographers sought out more editorial or abstract shots.

“What are you doing to set your work apart from the other two dozen people standing next to you with the same camera pointed at the same model?” he says.

Of course, not everyone starts out with a unique visual style. That point of view can be built over time, with continued practice and evolving taste. Wang developed hers by treating her Instagram as a research platform, constantly studying other photographers’ campaigns and taking note of what she liked and disliked.

You Need To Hustle

Unsurprisingly, hustling was also essential to these photographers’ success. To find out where fashion shows were taking place, Bassini tracked hairdressers and makeup artists who geotagged their locations online. White, in addition to scoping out fashion week show locations to capture street style, picked up assistant gigs and retouched for other photographers to pay the bills. “Alongside that, I was constantly making my own work and trying to build a portfolio I could eventually pitch with,” she says. “It was a slow process of cold emailing, coffee chats, meeting people on set and collaborating on as many tests and personal projects as possible.”

For Wang, hustling meant taking a series of strategic steps, beginning with her Instagram. After archiving old posts and curating her grid, she would monitor what other photographers were putting out to identify who the decision-makers were, so she could connect with them. “You need a portfolio first and foremost — and good work,” she explains. “But beyond that, you have to be pretty savvy about who needs to see that work for it to go somewhere.”

Don’t Give Up

At the end of the day, what sets these photographers apart is that they never quit, regardless of setbacks.

“[There are days] I woke up depressed and I didn’t want to do shit,” Gochez says. “But then I picked up the camera, and my creativity found me in the end. I think it’s like working out: It’s a muscle that you need to keep training.”

It’s hard to not take rejections personally. Wang reminded herself that art is subjective, which encouraged her to keep going. “Every mistake can be made to seem like a choice, too,” she says.

By using what was available to them, walking into rooms without invites, networking wisely and showing up consistently, these photographers forged their own paths in the competitive world of fashion photography. They serve as a reminder that there’s no singular right way to break in.

“For me, tenacity, kindness and a healthy amount of delusion have gone a surprisingly long way,” White says.

Weeks after the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s Costume Institute canceled its planned John Galliano exhibit for 2027, the infamous designer has successfully brought a different project to fruition: his debut Zara collection. Launching Thursday, “Vol. 1” of his two-year partnership includes outerwear, dresses, tees, suiting, knitwear, lingerie and accessories, all priced from $30 to $999. An accompanying campaign was photographed by Steven Meisel.

For the collection, titled “Re(form),” Galliano deconstructed and reimagined Zara’s “archives” (past collections) through techniques such as physical and digital hacking, shrinking, magnifying, swatching and splicing. For example, an “archival” coat is revamped into a net dress with faux fur trims; a shirt is graded up three times its original size to resemble a leather coat; two trousers are cut and repurposed into sans-culotte pants; and a lace shift dress is refashioned into a ruffled collar.

Deconstruction wasn’t the only theme on Galliano’s mind: The collection also drew inspiration from Les Incroyables and Les Merveilleuses, the defiant dandies and divas of post-Revolutionary France. They’re “evoked in contemporary guises through subversive and illusory compositions,” according to the brand. “In the process, they appear through alternate lenses: the bourgeois spirit of the gardening wardrobe, the cinematic glamour of film noir.” Their influence appears in the overcoats, breeches and frock coats.

Galliano’s Zara collaboration follows a years-long (and perhaps ongoing) effort to rehabilitate his image. In 2011, the designer was infamously caught on video spewing racist and antisemitic comments at Jewish and Asian patrons of a Paris café. He was quickly fired from his Dior gig, and later entered a drug and alcohol rehab program. Much of the fashion world has slowly welcomed him back: He quietly helped create Oscar de la Renta’s Fall 2013 collection and was hired by Maison Margiela as creative director the following year. (He resigned in December 2024). Celebrity stylists continue to dress their clients in Galliano’s designs, and his work had a major presence on the 2024 Met Gala red carpet.

Amid its own upmarket rebrand, Zara announced a two-year creative partnership with the designer in March 2026. Not long after, news broke that he would be the subject of next spring’s dedicated Costume Institute exhibit and Met Gala, but the plans were canceled just a month later due to significant backlash.

cachedArticles.title: Must Read: Roger Lynch Steps Down as Condé Nast CEO, Oura Delays IPO
cachedArticles.author: Neia Dizon
cachedArticles.snippet: Plus, Stride Consumer Partners raises $550 million for second fund.
cachedArticles.content:
These are the stories making headlines in fashion on Wednesday.

Roger Lynch Steps Down as Condé Nast CEO

Condé Nast CEO Roger Lynch is leaving after more than seven years to become CEO of Mattel, announcing the move in a statement Wednesday. “When I joined Condé Nast, I had the simple ambition to leave this extraordinary place stronger than I found it,” he wrote, noting that since 2020 commerce revenue grew 170%, digital subscriptions grew 155% and U.S. tentpole events increased ninefold. Lead Independent Director Mike Perlis will serve as interim CEO while a search for a permanent successor begins. {Condé Nast}

Oura Delays IPO

Oura is putting its initial public offering (IPO) on Nasdaq on hold, citing uncertainty in the IPO market even as the smart ring maker says its business is continuing to grow. Oura’s paid memberships have reached 5.7 million users, and revenue is expected to grow 90% year-over-year in fiscal 2026. Oura and its early investors had planned to sell 50 million shares at $40 to $44 each, which would have raised about $2.1 billion at the midpoint and valued the company at roughly $15 billion. {Business Wire; WWD/paywalled}

Stride Consumer Partners Raises $550 Million for Second Fund

Stride Consumer Partners — the backer of Odele, Crown Affair and Skinfix — has wrapped its second fund at $550 million, a 30% jump over its 2022 debut fund. The raise took roughly four months and leaned heavily on returning limited partners boosting their commitments. The investment firm’s assets under management are now about $1.3 billion. {Beauty Independent/paywalled}

Ralph Lauren To Stage First PoloFest in Tokyo

Ralph Lauren will hold PoloFest, a three-day celebration of Polo culture, from Oct. 23 to 25 at Jing Harajuku in Tokyo’s Shibuya district. The free event will feature an archival exhibition, a speaker series and a vintage marketplace with dealers from around the world. It also kicks off a series of global activations leading up to the brand’s 60th anniversary in 2027. {WWD/paywalled}

As fall’s crisp weather settles in and our appetite for pumpkin-flavored everything returns, team Fashionista is reflecting on the September beauty discoveries that earned a permanent spot on our vanities — and that helped us survive the New York Fashion Week hustle.

cachedArticles.author: Catie Pusateri
cachedArticles.snippet: Newcomers like Conner Ives and Magda Butrym also made waves for Spring 2027, according to analysis by Launchmetrics.
cachedArticles.content:
This season, the New York Fashion Week schedule boasted exciting debuts (Henry Zankov at Diane von Furstenberg), first-time runways (Conner Ives’ stateside homecoming) and plenty of drama (PETA v. Steven Kolb). But amid all the buzz, which brands ultimately came out on top?

On Tuesday, Launchmetrics released its Spring 2027 NYFW report, which details the event’s impactful “voices” (celebrities, media and influencers) and the top 20 power players by media impact value (MIV). This season, Launchmetrics also took its newest metric — AI visibility (AIV) — out for a spin: This measures a brand’s presence in AI-generated answers across ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Perplexity.

As a whole, NYFW generated a whopping $463 million MIV. In terms of format, social media placements drove 90% of the week’s total MIV at $416 million. Instagram dominated its fellow social platforms with its 55% share of MIV, but YouTube brought in more MIV per placement ($14K/placement, compared to Instagram’s $12K).

In terms of voices, 50% of total MIV came from media — meaning “any third-party entity publishing content written by media professionals” (so, Fashionista would be one example). After that, influencers contributed 28%, celebrities 10%, owned media 7% and partners (brands and retailers) 5%. As for Spring 2027’s top voices overall, Vogue U.S. once again reigned supreme ($13.2 million MIV), followed by Calvin Klein ($8.6 million MIV), Heart Evangelista ($7.6 million MIV), InStyle ($7.4 million MIV) and Mickey Blank ($6.9 million MIV).

View the 2 images of this gallery on the original article

Brand-wise, Tommy Hilfiger rose to the front of the fashion pack by raking in $58 million total MIV after taking a couple of years off from NYFW. (You may remember its previous venue: the Staten Island Ferry.) Calvin Klein came in second place with $47 million MIV, followed by Carolina Herrera with $20 million, Tory Burch with $19 million and Michael Kors with $16 million in MIV. H&M-owned retailer Cos, whose show was the site of that infamous PETA v. Steven Kolb altercation, took sixth place with $14 million in MIV. (It’s unclear how much of that was driven by the incident.)

Some surprising additions to the power-player list include Conner Ives ($5.6 million MIV) and Magda Butrym ($4.6 million MIV), both of whom made their NYFW debuts this season. Sabyasachi — an Indian luxury house founded by Sabyasachi Mukherjee in 1999 — also showed up on the list after returning to NYFW for the first time in 20 years, bringing in $5.3 million MIV.

As for the labels leading mentions on AI platforms, Diane von Furstenberg held the top position every day of NYFW, ending with an overall 9.9% share of AIV. The vast majority of these AI mentions centered around the label’s comeback, courtesy of Zankov, rather than the actual clothes themselves. Proenza Schouler came in second place with a 7.1% share of AIV, and it was the only label where critic reviews made up the largest share of AI coverage (22%), per the report.

cachedArticles.title: Must Read: Scarlett Johansson's The Outset Is Closing, Fashion Designer Sues Lego Over 'Queer Eye' Figurine's Jacket
cachedArticles.author: Neia Dizon
cachedArticles.snippet: Plus, luxury brands embrace youth culture as Gen Z spending slows.
cachedArticles.content:
These are the stories making headlines in fashion on Tuesday.

Scarlett Johansson’s Skin-Care Line The Outset Is Closing

The Outset, the skin-care line Scarlett Johansson co-founded in 2022, is shutting down, according to a notice on its website Monday. “Online shopping at theoutset.com has now ended, but all existing orders will continue to be processed as usual,” the brand stated on its website. The skin-care brand, sold at Sephora, Goop and Nordstrom, is the latest celebrity-linked beauty label to falter as shoppers turn to ingredient-driven products and cheaper Korean brands. {The Outset; Business of Fashion/paywalled}

Fashion Designer Sues Lego Over ‘Queer Eye’ Figurine’s Jacket

Fashion designer James Concannon has filed a lawsuit in Connecticut accusing Lego of copying a custom leather jacket he made for “Queer Eye” star Antoni Porowski. A miniature jacket marked with a peace sign and a skull appears on a figurine in Lego’s “Queer Eye – The Fab 5 Loft” set, which came out in September 2021. Concannon claims that Lego never asked for his authorization or paid him. He is now seeking damages for willful infringement. {CNN}

Luxury Brands Embrace Youth Culture as Gen Z Spending Slows

Some luxury houses are trading polish for a messier, youth-driven look, with Prada, Diesel and Burberry all leaning into grungy styling this season. This move follows Gen Z shoppers pulling back on luxury spending. Forecasters say the generation could account for 25-30% of U.S. luxury purchases by 2030. Some experts note a one-off subculture reference won’t work, since young consumers spot it quickly and expect brands to build trust first, possibly through cheaper entry products and music tie-ins. {Vogue Business}

M&S Partners With Sephora

Marks & Spencer has partnered with Sephora to sell the beauty retailer’s products in M&S stores and online as part of its push into beauty. Sephora shop-in-shops will open at 100 locations across the U.K., and M&S.com will carry a wider range with home delivery and in-store pickup. M&S holds just 1.3% of the £5.2 billion ($6.9 billion) British beauty market, which grew 1.2% in the year to July 19. The final brand line-up will be announced closer to launch. {Reuters/paywalled}

Unilever Says Wellness and Beauty Are Becoming More Intertwined

At the Groceryshop conference in Las Vegas, Unilever Wellbeing CEO Jostein Solheim said that consumers increasingly view beauty and health as one category, driven by GLP-1 drugs, AI health tools and easier access to scientific information. Alongside that, Gen Z and millennial shoppers are leading demand by focusing on longevity earlier in life. When Gap Inc. Creative Director Zac Posen began building Old Navy’s designer collaboration program, one of his top priorities was highlighting American talent. “I thought the American industry needed it, and we have such incredible talent here,” he tells Fashionista.

Anna Sui was the first label to participate in the program, followed by Christopher John Rogers. This fall, Old Navy tapped Altuzarra as its third designer collaborator. “Joseph [Altuzarra] has really built an incredible world, and he has a great sense of care,” Posen says. “He understands the joy and whimsy of our Old Navy customer.” There’s also a high-profile campaign star in the mix: Alexa Chung.

The collaboration came about organically, according to Joseph Altuzarra: “It was a really exciting opportunity to bring the storytelling and world of Altuzarra to the Old Navy customer.” His creative process began the same way he approaches his runway collections: with literature. Specifically, he referenced “Wuthering Heights” (as he did for Fall 2025) and “Pride and Prejudice.”

“I was really inspired by this romantic heroine, these windswept moors and this deep romanticism,” the designer explains. The lineup reflects the romance and mystery of classic fiction through vintage-inspired floral prints, rich jewel tones, Fair Isle sweaters and structured outerwear. However, it blends that literary attitude with Old Navy’s heritage of easy dressing, accessibility and versatile styles.

The limited-edition collection spans outerwear, dresses, tanks, blouses, jeans, trousers and accessories priced from $25 to $140. This is also the first designer collaboration that offers matching styles for girls and toddlers. Standout pieces include a parka with a detachable plaid liner; an embroidered, corduroy-collared jacket; high-waist balloon trousers and scarf dresses. As a cheeky reference to the literary theme, all of the clothing tags double as bookmarks.

“From the very beginning, [this collection] was a dialogue between what we do at Altuzarra — the romanticism, femininity and storytelling of the brand — [and] what Old Navy stands for, which is optimism and ease of American sportswear, and how those two things can come together,” Altuzarra says.

cachedArticles.title: 7 Spring 2027 Trends to Know From Milan Fashion Week
cachedArticles.author: Janelle Sessoms
cachedArticles.snippet: Consider this a cheat sheet on what to add to that spring fashion inspo board.
cachedArticles.content:
Milan Fashion Week has a reputation for being one of the tamer fashion month events, with onlookers often expecting designers to present lineup after lineup of elevated workwear. (The street style crowd certainly got that memo.) For Spring 2027, while there were a few labels that lived up to that expectation (we’re looking at you, Giorgio Armani and Tod’s), others proved Italian fashion can also be bold, daring and unpredictable.

That unexpectedness especially showed up in a handful of our favorite trends: Standouts include a non-HR-approved skirt style, a triumphant return for Bermuda shorts and the enthusiastic endorsement of plaid as a spring print. Scroll through the galleries below for seven MFW Spring 2027 trends to know.

Pinking of You

The era of Barbie pink may be over, but designers aren't quite ready to move on from the color as a whole. In New York, mauve was the rosy shade of choice. On the Milan runways, soft pinks were the favored hue. Labels like Blumarine and Prada incorporated ballet pinks, while Moschino and Vivetta opted for lighter, paler shades.

Split Decision

Not a fan of bra top dressing? Allow Italian designers to introduce split-front tops into your spring closet. The navel-baring blouse allows you to show some skin while keeping it modest (ish). At The Attico and Blumarine, models walked the runway in tie-front versions, while Ferragamo and Gucci presented it as a styling hack for button downs.

Pencil Me In

Pencil skirts are known for being a Millennial-beloved, office-appropriate garment, but the versions on the Milan Spring 2027 runways got a sexy update. (Consider this the return of the office siren, minus the office.) At Ferragamo and MGSM, models strutted in sheer, knee-length skirts. Meanwhile, Prada and Max Mara favored skirts with a not-so-HR-friendly slit.

Not-So-Short Shorts

From Moschino to MSGM, Bermuda shorts are so back. The longer length shorts came in various versions on the Milan runways, from Giorgio Armani's tailored styles to Diesel's denim jorts to Venerdi Pomeriggio's Bermuda bloomers.

Hip, Hip, Hooray

Season after season, designers' favorite historical garment to modernize is corsetry. For Spring 2027, they shifted their attention to double-sided bustle, unveiling a slew of garments with exaggerated, padded hips. It's refreshing seeing designers introduce one way for women to take up more space, rather than shrink themselves to occupy less of it.

Ruffle Some Feathers

Feathers on the runway are hardly new, but for spring, Italian designers employed them as statement trims. Feathered borders were placed on coats at Blumarine and The Attico, skirts at Yulin Cashmere District and Moschino and as decorative embellishments at Venerdi Pomeriggio.

Well Plaid

Plaid typically leans more fall, but the Milan runways have decreed it a spring print. Less underground-rocker-girl and more modern prep student, the pattern appeared at Gucci, Dhruv Kapoor and Marni on midi skirts, blazers and shift dresses.

cachedArticles.content:
The Council of Fashion Designers of America (CFDA) announced on Monday that the search for its next CEO is officially underway. This move follows former CFDA President and CEO Steven Kolb’s resignation from the top post on Sept. 18 amid growing backlash surrounding his decision to physically restrain PETA protestors at COS’ Fall 2026 runway show. Kolb previously held the title for 20 years, meaning this leadership change will usher in a new era for the organization.

The CFDA’s Board of Directors tapped Karen Harvey Consulting Group to spearhead the search for its new CEO. During this transitional period, Hildy Kuryk will serve as interim CEO. Kuryk is the co-founder of Artemis Strategies, a boutique consultancy specializing in creative brand strategy. She is also a top-ranking Condé Nast alumna, as she previously served as executive director of communications at Vogue and Teen Vogue, working directly with Anna Wintour. She continues to oversee press and communications strategy on behalf of Condé Nast and Vogue for the Met Gala.

Prior to her experience in the fashion media landscape, Kuryk spent 15 years in professional politics, including serving under two U.S. presidents and as the Democratic National Committee’s national finance director. 

“As we begin the search for CFDA’s next CEO, the Board is focused on identifying a leader who can guide the organization into its next chapter,” CFDA Board Chairman Thom Browne said in a statement. “We are grateful to Hildy Kuryk for providing steady interim leadership and a strong connection between the Board and staff during this period.”

According to the CFDA, its CEO search will focus on “identifying a leader who can build on the CFDA’s mission to strengthen American fashion, support designers and advance the organization’s role across the industry.”

These are the stories making headlines in fashion on Monday.

Derek Lam Returns to Derek Lam 10 Crosby as Creative Director

After exiting Derek Lam 10 Crosby three years ago, Founder Derek Lam is returning to the brand as its creative director. The move comes five months after NYC Alliance acquired the label. Lam will present the label’s first collection under NYC Alliance for Fall 2027. “I am looking forward to building on the design philosophy of Derek Lam 10 Crosby while bringing a fresh perspective to the brand’s next chapter,” Lam said in a press statement. {Fashionista inbox}

Chanel Reveals Its Cruise 2027 Show Location

Matthieu Blazy will present his sophomore Chanel Cruise collection in Deauville on April 27. The French coastal town has historic ties to the brand, as it was where founder Gabrielle Chanel opened her first ready-to-wear store in 1912. {WWD/paywalled}

Why Edward Buchanan Started a Nonprofit to Help Black Creatives

Designer Edward Buchanan has opened The Situation, a self-funded nonprofit that supports underrepresented creatives, including people of color, queer and women artists. Based in Italy, The Situation will fund projects and host residency programs that let participants present exhibitions and showroom openings (for free). It will also connect creatives with industry mentors and resources. “I just want to see these creatives be able to exist and have legs within the businesses and practices they want to create while being the exact individual that they are,” Buchanan told Vogue Business. {Vogue Business/paywalled}

Beauty Platform Tresalis Acquires Vyrao

Tresalis, a new beauty platform backed by German investment firm Athos, has acquired British fragrance brand Vyrao. The deal’s financial terms have not been revealed. Vyrao’s founder, Yasmin Sewell, will remain at the brand in the newly created role of chief brand officer. She hopes the acquisition will position Vyrao more in the wellness space. {Business of Fashion/paywalled}

These are the stories making headlines in fashion on Friday.

McMullen Opens Flagship in San Francisco’s Union Square

Luxury boutique McMullen — founded by Sherri McMullen in 2007 — is opening a new flagship in San Francisco’s Union Square, designed by Gabriella Khalil with statement works by Aisling Camps and Mickalene Thomas. Located at 135 Maiden Lane, the 6,342-square-foot store opens to the public on Sept. 25. Stocked brands include Dries Van Noten, Diotima, Proenza Schouler, Christopher John Rogers, Burc Akyol, Tibi, Kallmeyer and Heirlome, among many others. {Fashionista inbox}

Beckham Brands Deliver Strong Growth Across Ventures

David and Victoria Beckham’s businesses both posted strong results for fiscal 2025. David’s DRJB Holdings saw revenue climb 20% to $110.5 million and net profit rise to $49.8 million, fueled by new deals with McDonald’s, Verizon and PepsiCo’s Lay’s ahead of the 2026 FIFA World Cup. Victoria Beckham Holdings Ltd. turned an operating profit of £7.3 million ($9.8 million) while revenue rose 15% to £129.8 million ($174 million), marking its fifth straight year of double-digit growth. Momentum has continued into 2026, with both brands expanding retail footprints across the U.S. and Europe. {WWD/paywalled}

Chanel Taps Lucia Pieroni To Head Makeup Creative Direction

Chanel has named Lucia Pieroni as its creative makeup director, effective September 2026. Pieroni will report to Simona Cattaneo, president of fragrance and beauty. Pieroni previously served as creative director of makeup at Clé de Peau Beauté from 2006 to 2019 and has worked alongside Matthieu Blazy since his debut Chanel fashion show in October 2025. “Being chosen to join Chanel is a great honor,” Pieroni said, calling it “a particularly exciting juncture in Chanel’s journey.” {Fashionista inbox}

Researchers Question Safety of Natural Fibers

Demand for natural fibers like cotton and wool is climbing as shoppers increasingly turn away from synthetics over chemical and microplastic concerns. But researchers say the fibers need closer study as manufacturers often treat cotton and wool with substances such as PFAS and antimicrobial coatings, and the fabrics shed microfibers that have turned up in oceans and human lungs. Scientists caution the research remains far less developed than work on synthetic pollution, and no clothing has been linked to illness in wearers. {The Wall Street Journal/paywalled}

Gucci’s New Sneakers Depart From Italian-Made Roots

Gucci has started labeling some new footwear “Made in China,” including a $1,000 sneaker from designer Demna, departing from its Italian heritage as it courts price-conscious shoppers. The brand says the move reflects a supplier’s technical expertise, though analysts warn it could lessen Gucci’s luxury positioning, a risk compounded by a 50% sales drop over three years and reported price cuts in key markets like China. {Reuters/paywalled}

Maya Crothers had plenty of luxurious skin-care options in her arsenal, but nothing worked in the harsh Jackson Hole weather and nothing offered her the “clean” options that she was so passionate about. So, she put her frustration, and her engineering mind, to work. Her goal was to produce skin care with a real dedication to performance and “clean,” loaded with dermatologist-grade performance ingredients and combined with elements of nature: clays, essential oils, herbal extracts and marine-based elements. And it had to work wherever she traveled. The result was Circcell — a hybrid of “Circle,” meaning whole and balanced, and “Cellular,” indicating real change. A performance-based, environmentally-sensitive, unparalleled experience that performs elegantly in any climate, adjusting to your needs.

Circcell is dedicated to transformation — with products that harness potent, “age-defying” ingredients and actives known to deliver results through performance-driven formulations. The resulting collection delivers a sensual experience with the world’s most high-performing experience, and with a nod to the world we live in.
